title: Advanced Tailoring & Pattern Making
subtitle: Draft sleeves, collars, princess lines and African silhouettes, fit complex bodies, grade across sizes and run professional production and client work.
description: This advanced hands-on course builds on basic block drafting. You will manipulate patterns into new styles, draft set-in sleeves and collars, draft iro and buba, kaftans and boubous, fit and alter patterns for complex bodies, build size charts and grade across a size range, and run production patterns, quality control and professional client orders.
outcomes: Take shape measurements and read posture to plan pattern changes before cutting
Manipulate blocks into yokes, gathers, flare and princess-line panels, and draft sleeves and collars that fit
Draft iro and buba, kaftan and boubou patterns, including gussets, side panels and embroidered necklines
Build your own size chart, write grade rules and grade a pattern across a size range
Run toile fittings, read drag lines and make full bust, sway back, shoulder and arm alterations
Produce production patterns and markers, run quality control and price and manage professional orders
audience: Tailors who can already draft a basic bodice and skirt block and want to work at a professional, production-ready level.
tools: Tape measure, 60 cm ruler, set square, French curve and hip curve (or a pattern master)
Drafting paper, pattern card, pencil, tracing wheel, awl and paper scissors
Calico for toiles, fabric shears, pins and chalk
Sewing machine (an overlocker is helpful), steam iron, press cloth and tailor's ham
Phone for photos, WhatsApp and a spreadsheet app such as Google Sheets

modules.title: The Professional Pattern Room: Tools, Fabric Behaviour and Workroom
modules.overview: Advanced work starts with precise tools, a workroom that moves garments in a clear order, and a deep understanding of how fabric behaves before you cut it. This module sets up the professional standard you will use for every draft, toile and production order in the rest of the course.

lessons.title: Precision drafting tools and how professionals use them
objectives: Name the drafting tools used for curves, notches and pattern marking and say what each one does
Choose between a pattern master, French curve and hip curve for a given line
Mark a finished pattern piece with notches, drill holes and grain line correctly
Plan a starter kit for a pattern room on a realistic budget

blocks.text: At basic level, a tape measure, chalk and scissors are enough. At advanced level, you are no longer only sewing clothes. You are **making patterns that must be repeated exactly**, sometimes for twenty aso-ebi guests or a boutique order of thirty pieces. Every curve must be smooth, every notch must match its partner, and every piece must carry the information a cutter needs. That accuracy comes from the right tools used the right way.

blocks.name: triangular-ruler
blocks.caption: Accurate right angles at centre front, centre back and hem are the first sign of a professional pattern.

blocks.text: Rulers and curves

head: Tool
What it does
Typical use in this course
rows: Long metal or clear ruler (60 to 100 cm)
Draws long straight lines without bending
Centre front, grain lines, side seams of kaftans and boubous
Squaring hem lines, waist lines and the crown line of a sleeve
Straight edge, curves and seam allowance guides in one tool
Armholes, necklines and adding allowance in one movement
Armhole bottom, neckline, collar points, crotch curve
Hip line of a skirt, side seams, princess seams
Bends to measure or copy a curve
Measuring armhole and neckline length on the paper

blocks.text: The rule of thumb: **use the longest curve that fits the line**. A short French curve on a long princess seam makes a wobbly line made of many small curves joined together. A hip curve makes one smooth sweep. For an armhole, start with the French curve at the underarm where the curve is tightest, then blend into the straighter part near the shoulder.
Marking and transfer tools

items: **Tracing wheel**: copies lines from one paper to another, or from a pattern to fabric with carbon paper. A smooth-edged wheel is gentler on fine lace and silk; a serrated wheel grips paper better.
**Pattern notcher**: cuts a small slot in the edge of the paper so the notch is felt as well as seen. A neat 3 to 5 mm snip with scissors also works.
**Awl or bradawl**: punches a small hole inside the pattern to mark dart points, pocket positions and bust points. These are called drill holes.
**Pattern card or manila**: heavier than drafting paper. Final production patterns are traced onto card so edges do not tear after many uses.
**Pattern hooks and a rail**: keep all pieces of one style together, hung by a hole punched near the top of each piece.

blocks.title: Drill holes sit inside the stitching line
blocks.text: Punch a dart point drill hole about 1 cm inside the true point, not on it. If the hole sits exactly on the point, the chalk mark or snip on the fabric can show through after sewing.
What every finished pattern piece must say

A pattern that only you can understand is a draft. A pattern a cutter can use without asking questions is a **finished pattern**. Write clearly, in pencil first, then in marker once it is tested. Use the same layout on every piece so your eye always finds the information in the same place.

blocks.title: Labels on a finished pattern piece
items: Style name or number
Piece name and size
Cut quantity and fold
Grain line arrow
Notches and drill holes
Seam allowance stated
blocks.caption: If any one of these is missing, the cutter has to guess, and guesses cost fabric.

blocks.text: The **grain line arrow** must run the full length of the piece, with arrow heads at both ends, so the cutter can measure from the selvedge at two points. The **cut quantity** is written as, for example, "Cut 2 self, cut 2 lining" or "Cut 1 on fold". Notches use a simple code: one notch on the front armhole, two notches on the back armhole. That way a front sleeve can never be sewn into a back armhole.

blocks.title: Worked example: building a pattern room kit
blocks.context: For example, Amaka in Onitsha has a basic sewing kit and wants to begin drafting and storing patterns properly. She has about 60,000 naira (approximate) to spend and buys from the market and online sellers.
steps: She lists what she already has: tape measure, chalk, dressmaker scissors, a 30 cm ruler.
She prioritises tools that change accuracy most: a 60 cm clear ruler, a set square, a French curve and a hip curve (or one pattern master that combines curves).
She adds a tracing wheel, an awl, paper scissors kept only for paper, and a roll of drafting paper.
She buys a few sheets of manila card only for patterns she has already tested in a toile, so she does not waste card on drafts.
She prices each item at two shops and records the totals in a notebook. Prices vary a lot between Onitsha main market and online sellers, so she checks before buying.
blocks.result: Amaka has the tools for precise curves, marking and storage, and a written list with real prices she found. She keeps her fabric scissors away from paper so they stay sharp.

blocks.title: Two pairs of scissors
blocks.text: Paper blunts fabric shears quickly. Tie a ribbon on your fabric scissors and tell everyone in the workroom never to use them on paper, card or plastic.

Finally, keep a **pattern register**: a notebook or a simple spreadsheet listing each style, the sizes you have, the date of the last change and where the pattern hangs. When a client returns after a year asking for "the same buba as last time", you will find it in a minute.

takeaways: Use the longest curve that fits the line for smooth seams
Notches, drill holes and grain lines carry information the cutter needs
Every finished piece states style, piece, size, cut quantity, grain and allowance
Trace only tested patterns onto card and keep a pattern register

activity.title: Label a finished pattern piece
steps: Take any pattern piece you already use, for example a skirt front.
Redraw its curves with the correct curve tool so each line is one smooth sweep.
Add a full-length grain line with arrows at both ends.
Add notches (single at front, double at back where relevant) and drill holes 1 cm inside dart points.
Write the style name, piece name, size, cut quantity and seam allowance in one corner.
Start a pattern register page with this piece as the first entry.
activity.evidence: Photo of the labelled pattern piece and the first page of your pattern register

lessons.title: Fabric behaviour: grain, bias, shrinkage and difficult fabrics
objectives: Identify lengthwise grain, crosswise grain and true bias on any fabric
Run and calculate a shrinkage test before cutting
Plan motif placement for lace and border prints
Adjust handling for sequinned, sheer and slippery fabrics

blocks.text: Two garments cut from the same pattern can hang completely differently if the fabric behaves differently. Advanced tailors read the fabric before they cut it. This lesson covers the four things that most often ruin good patterns: grain, bias stretch, shrinkage and fabrics that move or fray.
Grain and bias

Woven fabric has long threads running parallel to the selvedge (the finished edge). This is the **lengthwise grain**, also called straight grain. It is the strongest direction and stretches least. The threads going across, from selvedge to selvedge, are the **crosswise grain**, which has a little more give. The diagonal at 45 degrees to both is the **true bias**. Fabric cut on the bias stretches and drapes much more.

blocks.title: Straight grain versus true bias
items: Straight grain
True bias
blocks.caption: Choose the grain on purpose: stability for structure, bias for drape.

blocks.text: To find true bias, fold the fabric so the crosswise edge lies along the selvedge. The fold line is the true bias. Bias strips for binding necklines and armholes are cut along this line. Bias-cut skirts and gowns should hang on a hanger for at least a day before you level the hem, because the bias drops unevenly as gravity pulls on it.
Shrinkage: test before you cut

Cotton, linen, many ankara prints and some locally woven fabrics shrink when first washed. If you cut a fitted gown to the exact size and the client washes it, it may become too tight. Always ask how the garment will be cleaned, then pre-treat the fabric the same way or test a sample.

items: Cut a square of 50 cm by 50 cm from the fabric, along the grain.
Mark the lengthwise direction with a thread or a pen arrow.
Wash and dry it the way the client will (hand wash and line dry, for example). Press it.
Measure both directions again.
Shrinkage percent = (before minus after) divided by before, times 100.

blocks.title: Worked example: shrinkage on a cotton print
blocks.context: For example, Bisi in Ibadan is making a fitted dress from a cotton print. She tests a 50 cm square before cutting.
steps: After washing, the lengthwise side measures 48.5 cm and the crosswise side 49.5 cm.
Lengthwise shrinkage: (50 minus 48.5) divided by 50 times 100 = 3 percent.
Crosswise shrinkage: (50 minus 49.5) divided by 50 times 100 = 1 percent.
A 110 cm dress length would lose about 3.3 cm in length after the first wash if not pre-washed.
She decides to wash, dry and press the full fabric before cutting.
blocks.result: Because she tested, the dress keeps its length and fit after the client's first wash, and Bisi records "pre-wash, 3 percent length shrinkage" on the order card.

blocks.text: Lace, border prints and directional fabrics

items: **Corded and beaded lace**: lay out in a single layer, right side up, so you can see where motifs fall. Place the scalloped edge at the hem or sleeve end where possible, so you do not need to hem it.
**Border prints and aso-oke strips**: the pattern runs along one edge. Decide early whether the border goes at the hem, the sleeve or the neckline, and lay all pieces the same way.
**Directional prints and pile fabrics (velvet)**: use a "with nap" layout, meaning every piece points the same way up. This uses more fabric, so plan for it in your yardage.
**Matching**: for checks, stripes and large prints, match at centre front, side seams and where the sleeve meets the bodice at the front notch.

blocks.name: black-scissors
blocks.caption: Single-layer cutting gives you control of every motif on lace and border prints.

blocks.text: Sequins, sheers and slippery fabrics

For **sequinned fabric**, remove sequins from the seam allowance before sewing, otherwise the needle breaks and the seam looks lumpy. Hand-stitch a few loose sequins back over bald areas after sewing. For **chiffon and organza**, cut between two layers of paper or on a fabric covered table so the fabric does not slide, use fine pins in the seam allowance only, and choose French seams so raw edges do not show through. For **satin and silky polyester**, use a fine sharp needle and test pressing temperature on a scrap, because these fabrics can melt or shine.

Before cutting any expensive fabric, check it on a light table or against a window for flaws: thin places, dye spots, pulled threads or misprints. Mark each flaw with a safety pin or a chalk circle on the wrong side, then lay your pieces so the flaws fall in the seam allowance or in waste. If a client brought the fabric, show her the flaw before you cut and note it on her order card, so nobody blames the cutting later.

blocks.title: Heat and synthetics
blocks.text: Many glittery and shiny fabrics are polyester or nylon and can melt under a hot iron. Always test on a scrap, use a press cloth, and keep the iron moving. Switch off and unplug the iron when you leave the table.

takeaways: Lengthwise grain is stable; true bias drapes and stretches
Test shrinkage on a 50 cm square and calculate the percent before cutting
Plan motif and border placement before any piece is cut
Sequins, sheers and satins each need their own handling

activity.title: Fabric behaviour test card
steps: Choose two fabrics you use often, for example an ankara and a lace.
Mark straight grain and true bias on a scrap of each and pull gently to feel the difference.
Run a 50 cm shrinkage test on the washable fabric and calculate both percentages.
Write a card for each fabric: fibre (if known), shrinkage, iron setting that worked, needle used, special handling.
Staple a small swatch to each card.
activity.evidence: Two fabric test cards with swatches and shrinkage calculations

lessons.title: Setting up a production-ready workroom: machines, flow and electrical safety
objectives: Arrange a workroom so garments move in one direction from cutting to packing
Compare a domestic machine, an industrial straight stitch and an overlocker
Apply electrical safety rules for machines, irons and generators
Set up light and seating that protect your eyes and back

blocks.text: When orders grow, the problem is rarely sewing skill. It is **flow**: fabric piled on the machine table, pattern pieces lost under offcuts, a client waiting while you look for her measurement card. A production-ready workroom arranges the work so each garment moves forward, never backwards.

blocks.title: One-way workroom flow
items: Receive and record fabric
Cut and bundle
Sew
Press and finish
Inspect and pack
blocks.caption: Arrange tables in this order so work moves forward and nothing doubles back.

blocks.text: Zones and bundles

items: **Receiving shelf**: every client's fabric is tagged with name, order number and due date the moment it arrives.
**Cutting table**: the largest clear surface. Nothing else lives here. Hip height is kindest to your back.
**Bundling**: after cutting, tie all pieces of one garment together with its order tag. Include the trims (zip, buttons, lining) in the bundle so the sewer never searches.
**Sewing zone**: machines with good light. Keep a small bin for threads and offcuts at each machine.
**Pressing zone**: iron, board, tailor's ham, sleeve board and press cloths, close to the sewing zone because you press after almost every seam.
**Finishing and packing**: hand sewing, buttons, final inspection, hanger and garment bag.

blocks.name: my-workspace
blocks.alt: A person working at an organised workstation
blocks.caption: An organised station saves minutes on every garment, and minutes add up to orders.

blocks.text: Choosing machines

head: Machine
Strengths
Limits
rows: Slower, can struggle with thick layers and long runs
Fast, strong, very even stitches, built for daily long use
One stitch type, needs a table and more space
Trims and finishes edges in one pass, essential for knits and clean insides
Cannot replace a lockstitch for main seams on woven fabrics

blocks.text: Industrial machines come with either a **clutch motor**, which runs all the time once switched on and can feel hard to control, or a **servo motor**, which only runs when you press the pedal, is quieter, and lets you set a slower speed. For a home workroom with unstable power, a servo motor is usually easier to control and uses less electricity because it is not running while you pin or press.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a two-machine workroom
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa in Kaduna sews about six garments a week on one domestic machine and wants to double output for wedding season.
steps: She times herself: finishing seams by zigzag takes about 25 minutes per gown.
She adds an overlocker, which finishes edges as it sews. Finishing drops to about 8 minutes per gown in her test.
On 12 gowns a week that saves about 17 minutes times 12, which is over 3 hours a week.
She keeps the domestic machine for buttonholes and decorative stitches and saves toward an industrial straight stitch for main seams.
She moves her pressing board next to the machines so she does not walk across the room after each seam.
blocks.result: Hauwa invests in the machine that removes her slowest step first, and rearranges the room so the work flows forward. The time figures are her own measurements, which is how you should decide too.

blocks.text: Electrical safety

blocks.title: Power rules for the workroom
blocks.text: Do not plug several machines and an iron into one extension board; irons draw a lot of current and overloaded boards can overheat. Use a voltage stabiliser or surge protector for machines. Run generators outside, never in a closed room, because exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which can kill without warning. Unplug the iron when not in use, keep cables out of walkways, and switch off a machine before changing the needle or clearing a jam.
Light and posture

Dark thread on dark fabric under a weak bulb causes crooked seams and tired eyes. Put a bright, white LED lamp at each machine and over the cutting table. Sit so your elbows are about level with the machine bed and your feet rest flat on the pedal. Every hour, stand, stretch your neck and shoulders, and look at something far away for a minute. A tailor with back pain cannot deliver on time.

Plan for power cuts too. Keep a rechargeable lamp at the cutting table so a blackout never catches you halfway through a cut, and do your heaviest pressing when you have steady supply. Some tailors batch all pressing for the day into one session on the generator or when grid power returns, which saves fuel. Keep fuel stored in a proper container, outside and away from the generator while it is hot.

Write your workroom rules on one sheet and stick it on the wall: where fabric is received, how bundles are tagged, power rules, and the end-of-day routine (unplug, clear tables, hang patterns). Anyone who helps you, an apprentice or a family member, follows the same sheet.

takeaways: Arrange the workroom so garments move forward from receiving to packing
Bundle all pieces and trims of a garment with its order tag
Add the machine that removes your slowest step first
Never run a generator indoors and never overload an extension board

activity.title: Map and fix your workroom
steps: Draw a simple floor plan of your current space with tables, machines and sockets.
Draw arrows showing how one garment moves from fabric to packing. Mark any place it goes backwards.
Time one full garment and note your slowest step.
Redraw the plan in one-way order and list any electrical fixes needed.
Write your one-page workroom rules sheet.
activity.evidence: Before and after floor plan, timing note and workroom rules sheet

lessons.title: Interfacing, linings and care labelling for client garments
objectives: Choose woven, non-woven or knit fusible interfacing for collars, facings and plackets
Fuse interfacing correctly and test it on a scrap
Select a lining that suits the fashion fabric and the climate
Write a care label using the five international care symbol shapes

blocks.text: The parts of a garment the client never sees decide whether it still looks good after ten wears. Collars that curl, facings that roll out and gowns that cling to the body usually come from the wrong interfacing or lining, not from bad sewing. This lesson covers the hidden layers and how to tell the client how to care for the result.
Interfacing: the skeleton of collars and facings

Interfacing is an extra layer that adds firmness. **Fusible** interfacing has glue on one side and is ironed on. **Sew-in** interfacing is stitched in place and suits fabrics that cannot take heat or that would bubble with glue, such as some sequinned or very fine fabrics.

head: Type
Behaviour
Good for
rows: Has a grain like fabric, moves naturally
Shirt collars and stands, cuffs, plackets, tailored jackets
Small areas, waistbands, bag making; can feel stiff on fine fabric
Knit fabrics, soft facings, lightweight blouses

blocks.text: Match the weight: interfacing should be the same weight or lighter than the fashion fabric. Cut woven interfacing on the same grain as the piece it supports. For collars, many tailors interface only the **upper collar** or only the **under collar** depending on the look they want; test both on scraps to see which gives the roll you like.

items: Cut a test piece of fabric and interfacing, about 15 cm square.
Place glue side (the rough or shiny dots) down on the wrong side of the fabric.
Cover with a damp press cloth. Press down firmly without sliding, holding for about 10 to 15 seconds, then lift and move to the next spot.
Let it cool flat before moving it, because the glue sets as it cools.
Check: no bubbles, no glue on the right side, no shine or puckering. If it fails, change temperature or interfacing.

blocks.name: coat
blocks.caption: The crisp collar and front of a tailored garment depend on the right interfacing underneath.

blocks.text: Linings for comfort and finish

A lining hides seams, stops lace from scratching, and helps a gown hang smoothly. In warm climates, breathable linings feel far better against the skin. Cotton lawn or cotton voile breathe well; polyester linings are cheaper and slide easily but can feel hot. For lace and sheer fabric, the lining colour changes the look completely: a nude or skin-tone lining makes lace look delicate, while a contrasting lining makes the pattern of the lace stand out. Show the client both options against the lace before cutting.
Care symbols: the five shapes

International care symbols are set out in the standard **ISO 3758**, maintained with input from GINETEX, the European textile care labelling association. There are five basic shapes. Dots inside the iron show temperature: one dot means low (about 110 degrees C), two dots medium (about 150 degrees C), three dots high (about 200 degrees C). A bar under a symbol means a gentler treatment and two bars mean very gentle. A cross through any symbol means do not.

blocks.title: The five care symbol shapes
items: Washtub: washing
Triangle: bleaching
Square: drying
Iron: ironing
Circle: professional cleaning
blocks.caption: Every care label is built from these five shapes plus dots, bars and crosses.

blocks.title: Worked example: a care card for a lined lace gown
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma in Enugu finishes a corded lace gown lined in polyester, with a concealed zip and some hand-sewn beads.
steps: She tests a lace scrap: beads loosen in a machine wash, so she chooses hand wash cold, or professional dry cleaning.
Bleach would discolour the lace, so the triangle gets a cross.
Tumble drying could melt the polyester lining, so she writes "dry flat in shade".
Her pressing test worked at one dot on the wrong side with a cloth, so she adds the one-dot iron symbol and "press on the reverse".
She writes the card in plain words under each symbol, because many clients do not know the symbols.
blocks.result: The client receives a small printed card with symbols and words. If the gown is damaged by a hot iron later, Ifeoma has clear proof she gave correct instructions.

blocks.title: Words plus symbols
blocks.text: Always add plain words under each symbol, and send the same care note on WhatsApp with the delivery photo. The client then has it on her phone when the house help is ironing.

Keep a small stock of your best interfacing and linings, labelled by weight and colour, so you are not forced to buy whatever a market stall has on the day before a deadline. Record which combinations worked on each fabric in the test cards from the previous lesson.

takeaways: Match interfacing type and weight to the fabric, and always test on a scrap
Fuse by pressing without sliding, then let it cool flat
Choose breathable linings for comfort and the lining colour on purpose
Care labels use five shapes from ISO 3758; add plain words for clients

activity.title: Interfacing and care card test
steps: Fuse two different interfacings onto scraps of the same fabric.
Make a small collar sample with each and compare roll and stiffness.
Choose a garment you made recently and write a care card with symbols and plain words.
Send yourself the care note as a WhatsApp message to check how it reads on a phone.
activity.evidence: Two labelled collar samples and one written care card

quiz.q: Ada is drawing a long princess seam from shoulder to hem. Which tool will give the smoothest line?
options: A hip curve or long curve section of a pattern master
A small French curve, moved many times
A tape measure held by hand
quiz.explain: Use the longest curve that fits the line. A hip curve makes one smooth sweep, while a small French curve moved many times creates a wobbly line.

quiz.q: A 50 cm square of cotton measures 48 cm lengthwise after washing. What is the lengthwise shrinkage?
quiz.explain: (50 minus 48) divided by 50 times 100 = 4 percent.

quiz.q: Why is it wise to hang a bias-cut skirt for a day before levelling the hem?
options: To let the colour fade evenly
To make the zip easier to insert
Because bias-cut fabric drops unevenly as gravity pulls on it
Because the interfacing needs to cool
quiz.explain: Bias stretches more than straight grain and drops unevenly. Levelling after hanging gives a straight hem that stays straight.

quiz.q: Funmi has five machines, a steam iron and one extension board. What should she do?
options: Plug everything into the board to save sockets
Run the generator inside the workroom so the cable is short
Only switch off at the end of the week
Spread the load across sockets and use a stabiliser or surge protector, keeping the iron separate
quiz.explain: Irons draw a lot of current and overloaded boards can overheat. Spread the load, protect machines and never run a generator indoors.

quiz.q: What does one dot inside an iron care symbol mean?
quiz.explain: One dot is low (about 110 degrees C), two dots medium (about 150), three dots high (about 200).

quiz.q: Kemi's fusible interfacing bubbled after washing. What is the most likely cause?
options: She pressed without sliding and let it cool
She slid the iron, used too little heat or pressure, or skipped testing
She cut the interfacing on grain
quiz.explain: Bubbling usually comes from poor fusing: sliding, too little heat, pressure or time. Testing on a scrap first catches this.

quiz.q: Which machine finishes raw edges in the same pass as sewing a seam?
quiz.explain: An overlocker trims and wraps the edge with thread as it sews, which saves time on finishing.

modules.title: Measuring Complex Bodies and Building Size Charts
modules.overview: Basic measuring gets you close. Advanced measuring captures shape, posture and proportion, so the first toile is nearly right. In this module you take the extra measurements that pattern adjustments depend on, learn to read a figure respectfully, build your own size chart from real client data and check every number before it reaches paper.

lessons.title: Beyond the basic tape: shape measurements for advanced drafting
objectives: Take high bust, full bust, bust span and bust depth measurements correctly
Measure across back, across front, shoulder slope and armhole depth
Use the high bust to full bust difference to decide on a bust adjustment
Record measurements in a layout that supports later pattern changes

blocks.text: A basic measurement card has bust, waist, hip, lengths and perhaps a shoulder. That is enough for loose styles. For fitted gowns, princess lines and set-in sleeves, those numbers hide important information. Two women with a 100 cm bust can need completely different patterns: one may have a broad back and small bust, the other a narrow back and a full bust. Shape measurements reveal the difference.

blocks.name: straight-ruler
blocks.caption: Shape measurements tell you where the body carries its width, not only how wide it is.

blocks.text: Bust measurements that drive fit

head: Measurement
How to take it
What it tells you
rows: Tape high under the arms, above the fullest part of the bust, flat across the back
The frame size: shoulders, upper chest and back
Tape over the fullest part of the bust, level all round
Total width needed at bust level
Straight across between the two bust points
Where dart points and princess seams should aim
From the high shoulder point near the neck, down to the bust point
How low the bust sits; sets dart and seam height
Snug, directly under the bust, level
Empire lines, corset bodices, bra fitting of gowns

blocks.text: The **difference between full bust and high bust** is one of the most useful numbers in fitting. When it is large, the body is proportionally fuller at the bust than the frame. If you draft only from full bust, the shoulders and neckline become too wide and the armhole gapes. Experienced pattern makers often draft the frame from the high bust and then add bust room where it is needed, using a full bust adjustment, which you will practise in Module 5.
Back, shoulder and arm measurements

items: **Across back**: from armhole crease to armhole crease, about 10 to 12 cm below the nape, with arms relaxed. Too small a pattern here causes pulling across the back when she reaches forward.
**Across front**: crease to crease at the front, a few centimetres above the bust.
**Shoulder length**: from the side of the neck to the shoulder bone.
**Shoulder slope**: note whether shoulders are square, average or sloping. Some tailors measure from the nape around to the shoulder tip and down to the waist at front and back to capture it.
**Armhole depth and armscye**: around the arm at the armpit crease, plus the vertical distance from the shoulder to the underarm level.
**Upper arm (bicep)**: at the fullest part with the arm relaxed, then again with the elbow bent. Large upper arms need a sleeve adjustment.
**Nape to waist** and **front neck to waist** (centre front), to catch posture differences.

blocks.title: Measure the bra she will wear
blocks.text: Bust point height and span change with the bra. Ask the client to wear the bra she plans to wear with the garment, especially for wedding and owambe gowns.

blocks.title: From measurements to a bust decision
items: Measure high bust
Measure full bust
Find the difference
Small: draft as normal
Large: draft frame, add bust
blocks.caption: The high bust to full bust difference tells you whether to adjust for the bust.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a client's numbers
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi in Port Harcourt measures a client for a fitted corset-style gown. High bust 92 cm, full bust 104 cm, across back 36 cm, bust span 20 cm, bust depth 27 cm.
steps: Full bust minus high bust = 104 minus 92 = 12 cm. This is a large difference.
She notes that the frame (shoulders and back) is closer to a 92 cm body than a 104 cm body.
She plans to draft the bodice frame from the smaller measurement and add bust width with a bust adjustment.
Bust span of 20 cm means each bust point sits 10 cm from centre front; she marks this on the pattern.
Bust depth of 27 cm sets the bust point height, so darts and princess seams aim at the right place.
blocks.result: Instead of a gown with a gaping neckline and wide shoulders, Ngozi's first toile sits correctly on the frame and has room exactly where the bust needs it.

blocks.text: Take every shape measurement with the client standing in her normal posture, wearing thin fitted clothing, and with the tape snug but not pressing into the body. For lengths, tie a narrow tape or elastic around the natural waist first, so every vertical measurement ends at the same line. Mark the bust point lightly with a small sticker or a chalk dot on her clothing if she agrees, so the span and depth readings start from the same spot each time. If something is hard to measure alone, such as across back on a client with long braids, ask her to hold her hair up or ask an assistant to help.

Record measurements to the nearest half centimetre and always in the same order. A card with the order bust group, back group, arm group, length group means you can scan it quickly and spot a missing number before the client leaves.

takeaways: Shape measurements reveal where the body carries width
The high bust to full bust difference guides bust adjustments
Across back, shoulder slope and bicep prevent pulling and tight sleeves
Measure in the bra she will wear and record in a fixed order

lessons.title: Reading the figure: posture, proportion and respectful observation
objectives: Recognise common posture variations such as sway back, rounded back and erect posture
Note shoulder, seat and abdomen shape that change the pattern
Take reference photos with consent and store them securely
Talk about body shape in neutral, professional language

blocks.text: Numbers tell you size. Your eyes tell you shape. Two clients with identical measurements can stand very differently: one leans back, one rounds her shoulders forward, one carries more on the seat, another more in front. These differences decide where wrinkles will appear on the finished garment. Advanced tailors observe them at the measuring stage and plan the pattern changes before cutting.
Look from three sides

Ask the client to stand naturally, feet slightly apart, arms relaxed, looking straight ahead. Do not ask her to stand up straight; you want her normal posture, because that is how she will wear the garment. Look from the front, the side and the back, and write short notes.

head: What you see
Name
Likely pattern effect
rows: Deep hollow at the lower back, seat prominent
Horizontal folds above the back waist; back waist length needs shortening
Upper back curved forward, head forward
Back pulls up, hem rises at back; needs more back length and width at upper back
Front needs more length, back may need less
One shoulder lower than the other
Different shoulder slope on left and right; pad or adjust one side
Front hem rises, side seams swing forward; front needs extra length and width
Back skirt rides up; back needs extra length and dart depth

blocks.name: trying-on-clothes
blocks.alt: A woman trying on clothes in front of a mirror
blocks.caption: Observing how a client stands naturally lets you predict where a garment will pull or fold.

blocks.title: Figure observation checklist
items: Shoulders: square, average, sloping
Back: straight, rounded, sway
Bust: high, average, low
Abdomen and seat shape
Left and right differences
blocks.caption: Tick each line at the measuring stage so pattern changes are planned, not discovered.

blocks.text: Simple checks that need no special tools

items: **Side seam check**: tie a narrow elastic or tape around the waist. From the side, look at whether it sits level. If it dips at the back, there may be a sway back; if it dips at the front, there may be a full abdomen pulling it down.
**Plumb line**: hang a weighted thread from the ear lobe at the side. Note where it falls relative to the shoulder, hip and ankle. This shows forward or backward lean.
**Shoulder level**: stand behind and place a ruler across both shoulder tips; see whether it tilts.
**Neck**: note a forward head or a thick neck base, which affect the back neckline and collars.

blocks.text: Photos with consent and privacy

Front, side and back photos help you check observations later and compare toile fittings. Only take them with clear permission, in fitted everyday clothing, never undressed. Explain why you want them and how you will store them. Keep them in a locked folder, not in your general gallery that syncs to shared devices, and never post them or send them to anyone else. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets duties for anyone handling personal data, and body photos are among the most personal. Delete them when the order is complete unless the client agrees you keep them for future orders.

Not every observation needs a pattern change. Small differences, such as a few millimetres between shoulders, disappear in a loose kaftan and only matter in fitted styles. Decide which observations matter for the style she ordered, and focus your notes there. A fitted corset bodice is affected by almost everything on the checklist; a flowing boubou is affected mainly by shoulder slope and uneven shoulders, because the garment hangs from the shoulders.

blocks.title: Respectful language
blocks.text: Use neutral pattern words, not judgements. Say "your back has a lovely curve, so I will shorten the back waist to stop folds" rather than "you have a big bottom". Clients return to tailors who make them feel respected.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning changes before cutting
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kano measures a client for a fitted lace bodice and a long pencil skirt. The numbers match a standard size, but her observation notes say: sway back, sloping shoulders, prominent seat.
steps: For the sway back, she plans to fold out about 1.5 cm at the centre back waist on the bodice, tapering to nothing at the side seam, and to test it in the toile.
For sloping shoulders, she plans to lower the shoulder point by about 1 cm and lower the underarm by the same amount to keep the armhole size.
For the prominent seat, she plans to deepen the back skirt darts slightly and add length at the centre back hem.
She writes each planned change and its amount on the order card, marked "to confirm at toile".
blocks.result: At the first fitting the toile already sits close to correct. The amounts are starting guesses, which the toile confirms or corrects, and she records the final amounts for the client's next order.

takeaways: Observe natural posture from front, side and back
Each posture variation predicts a specific pattern change
Take body photos only with consent and store them privately
Use neutral, respectful words when discussing body shape

lessons.title: Building your own size chart from real client data
objectives: Collect and organise measurements from past clients into a dataset
Choose a base size and size intervals that suit your market
Build a size chart with body measurements and finished garment measurements
Explain the difference between body measurements and garment measurements

blocks.text: If you supply boutiques, sell ready-made iro and buba sets online, or make uniforms, you need sizes, not just individual measurements. Imported size charts were built on other populations and often do not match your clients, especially at the hip. The professional solution is to **build your own chart from your own measurement records**. You already have the data on your client cards.

blocks.name: data-table
blocks.alt: A person working with a table of data
blocks.caption: Your client cards are a dataset; a size chart is that data organised.

blocks.text: Step 1: gather and clean the data

items: Copy bust, waist, hip, across back and key lengths from your client cards into a notebook table or a spreadsheet such as Google Sheets. Use first names or numbers only, not full names.
Remove obvious errors, such as a waist larger than the hip by 30 cm on a client you remember as pear-shaped. Re-check with the client if possible.
Sort the rows by bust (for tops) or by hip (for skirts and trousers).
Look at the range: smallest and largest values, and where most clients cluster.

blocks.text: Step 2: choose your base size and intervals

The **base size** is the size you draft and fit first, ideally the size your clients wear most often, because errors in fitting are smallest near the middle. The **interval** is the jump between sizes. Many charts use a jump of about 4 to 5 cm in bust, waist and hip between neighbouring sizes; larger sizes often use bigger jumps. There is no single correct number: use what your data shows. If your clients' hips are proportionally larger than their bust compared with an imported chart, your chart should show that.

blocks.title: From data to chart
items: Published size chart
Grade intervals chosen
Base size fitted
Clusters in the data
Clean client measurements
blocks.caption: A reliable chart is built from the bottom up, starting with clean real measurements.

blocks.text: Step 3: body chart and garment chart

A **body measurement chart** tells the buyer which size to choose: "if your bust is 96 to 100 cm, choose size 14". A **finished garment chart** tells you and the buyer the actual size of the item: "the size 14 buba measures 116 cm around the bust". The difference between them is the **ease**, and it changes by style. A fitted gown may have only a few centimetres of ease at the bust, while a buba has a lot. Always publish both when you sell online, because buyers then compare with a garment they already own.

blocks.title: Worked example: a four-size chart for ready-made buba sets
blocks.context: For example, Tola in Lagos has 60 past client cards and wants to sell ready-made iro and buba on Instagram and WhatsApp.
steps: She sorts by bust. Most clients fall between 92 and 112 cm, with the biggest cluster around 100 to 104 cm.
She sets her base size as the size for a 100 to 104 cm bust and calls it M.
She uses an interval of 5 cm and gets S (95 to 99), M (100 to 104), L (105 to 109), XL (110 to 114).
She checks hips in each bust group and sees they are on average larger than an imported chart suggests, so she sets her hip ranges from her own data.
She decides the buba should have 16 cm of ease at the bust and writes the finished bust: S 115, M 120, L 125, XL 130 cm (taking the top of each range plus ease).
She posts both charts together with a measuring guide.
blocks.result: Tola's chart reflects her real buyers, so returns and exchange requests are fewer. The ranges and ease figures are her own choices from her data, which is exactly how a chart should be made.

blocks.text: Lengths need sizes too. Check nape to waist, shoulder to floor and sleeve length in each size group. In many datasets height varies independently of width, so a tall size 10 and a short size 10 may both exist among your clients. You can handle this with a standard length plus a note that you will shorten or lengthen on request, or with separate regular and tall lengths if your data shows enough tall buyers to justify it.

blocks.title: Name sizes clearly
blocks.text: Clients may say "size 14" from UK labels or "L" from other brands, and these do not agree between brands. Publish centimetre ranges beside every size name so nobody guesses.

Review your chart every six months. Add new client data, and track exchanges: if many people who ordered L say it is tight at the hip, the hip range for L is wrong. A size chart is a living document, not a one-time task.

takeaways: Build size charts from your own client data, not imported charts
Choose a base size where most of your clients are
Publish both body measurements and finished garment measurements
Update the chart from exchange and return feedback

lessons.title: Verifying measurements: cross-checks, garment measuring and records
objectives: Use cross-checks to catch measurement errors before drafting
Measure a well-fitting garment and compare it with body measurements
Set tolerances for when a measurement must be retaken
Keep version-controlled client records that support repeat orders

blocks.text: Every advanced tailor has a story about a gown cut from one wrong number. A tired evening, a tape that slipped, a 7 written like a 1. The fix is not to measure more carefully once; it is to build **checks** into your routine that catch errors automatically, just as an accountant checks that totals add up.
Cross-checks that should add up

items: **Across front plus across back** should be noticeably less than the full bust, because neither includes the sides under the arms.
**Waist** is normally smaller than **hip**. If the waist is larger, re-check and confirm with your eyes: some bodies really are like that, but confirm.
**Nape to waist** and **front neck to waist** differ by a few centimetres on most bodies; a very large difference suggests posture or a measuring error.
**Left and right**: measure shoulder length and arm length on both sides once. Differences over about 1 cm are worth noting.
**Repeat the key three**: bust, waist and hip taken twice. If the two readings differ by more than about 1 cm, take a third.

blocks.name: verify-data
blocks.alt: A person verifying data on a screen
blocks.caption: Checking numbers against each other catches the errors that careful measuring alone misses.

blocks.title: Measurement verification loop
items: Measure
Cross-check totals
Compare with garment
Retake if outside tolerance
Record with date
blocks.caption: Run this loop before any number goes onto drafting paper.

blocks.text: Measuring a garment she loves

Ask the client to bring a garment that fits her well, in the same type of style. Lay it flat, button or zip it closed, and measure across the bust, waist and hip, doubling the flat measurement. Measure shoulder width, sleeve length, armhole and length. Compare with her body measurements. The difference is the ease she likes. This is powerful information, because ease preference is personal: some clients like a close fit, others like room to move and breathe in the heat.

blocks.title: Worked example: catching an error with a garment check
blocks.context: For example, Chioma in Abuja measures a client's bust at 98 cm and hip at 104 cm. The client brings a well-fitting fitted dress.
steps: Flat dress bust is 51 cm, so the circumference is 102 cm: ease of 4 cm over a 98 cm bust. Reasonable.
Flat dress hip is 50 cm, so 100 cm around. That is smaller than her measured 104 cm hip, which is impossible for a woven dress without stretch.
Chioma checks the fabric: it is a woven without stretch, so one number is wrong.
She re-measures the hip with the client standing with feet together and gets 98 cm. The first reading had the tape dipping at the back.
She corrects the card, notes the date, and adds 2 cm ease, matching the dress the client likes.
blocks.result: The garment check exposed a 6 cm error that would have produced a loose, baggy skirt. The client never knew there was a problem.

blocks.text: Tolerances and version-controlled records

A **tolerance** is the amount of difference you accept. For example, you might decide that a repeat bust reading within 1 cm is acceptable, but anything more is retaken. Write your tolerances on your card template so apprentices follow the same rule.

Some tailors also measure the client on two occasions before an important garment such as a wedding gown, a few weeks apart, because weight can change before big events. If the numbers move, use the latest set for the final fitting and keep the toile seams generous until the last fitting. Plan this into the timeline you agree with the client, so the extra measuring session is expected, not a surprise.

Bodies change with time, pregnancy, illness and age. Never overwrite old measurements. Add a new dated column each time you measure, so the card shows history. For repeat clients, re-measure the key three at every new order, even if she says nothing has changed. If you keep cards digitally, back them up and protect them with a password, and store only what you need: name, phone, measurements, notes on fit. Delete records of clients who ask you to.

Write numbers clearly and include units. Cross your sevens and write a full zero before the decimal point, for example 0.5 cm, not .5 cm. Small habits like these stop an apprentice from reading 1 for 7 or missing a decimal point when the card is copied into the pattern.

blocks.title: Fitting notes are gold
blocks.text: Add the final pattern changes from each fitting to the card, for example "sway back 1.5 cm, lower right shoulder 0.8 cm". Next time, these go straight onto the pattern before the first toile.

takeaways: Build cross-checks into every measuring session
Measure a well-fitting garment to learn her ease preference
Set a tolerance and retake readings that fall outside it
Keep dated measurement history and fitting notes; never overwrite

quiz.q: A client has a high bust of 88 cm and a full bust of 100 cm. What does this suggest?
options: Draft the whole bodice from 100 cm with no changes
Draft the frame from the smaller measurement and add bust room with an adjustment
Ignore the bust and use the waist
Use the hip measurement for the bodice
quiz.explain: A 12 cm difference shows the bust is full compared with the frame. Drafting only from 100 cm would make shoulders and neckline too wide.

quiz.q: From the side, a client's waist tape dips at the back and the lower back is deeply curved. What will a standard bodice show?
options: Horizontal folds just above the back waist
quiz.explain: This is a sway back. Excess back length collects as horizontal folds above the back waist, which is fixed by shortening the centre back waist.

quiz.q: Tola's buba must have 16 cm bust ease. What is the finished bust for a size whose body range tops out at 109 cm?
quiz.explain: Finished garment bust = body bust + ease = 109 + 16 = 125 cm.

quiz.q: Why should a seller publish a finished garment chart as well as a body chart?
options: Buyers can compare with a garment they already own and see the ease
It replaces the need for a body chart
quiz.explain: The garment chart shows the actual size of the item, so buyers can compare with clothes they own. The difference between charts is the ease.

quiz.q: A woven dress that fits a client measures 100 cm around the hip, but her measured hip is 104 cm. What should the tailor do?
options: Remeasure, because a non-stretch garment cannot be smaller than the body it fits
Cut the new dress at 100 cm without checking
quiz.explain: A woven garment without stretch must be larger than the body. One number is wrong, so remeasure before drafting.

quiz.q: Where should client body photos be kept?
options: In the general phone gallery that syncs to family devices
Posted to a WhatsApp status so the client can see them
In a private, protected folder, with consent, deleted when no longer needed
Sent to other tailors for advice without asking
quiz.explain: Body photos are highly personal data. Take them only with consent, store privately, never share, and delete when no longer needed.

quiz.q: A returning client says she has not changed size. What is the best practice?
options: Overwrite the old numbers with guesses
Ask her to measure herself and send it later
Re-measure at least bust, waist and hip and add a new dated column
quiz.explain: Bodies change. Re-measure the key three and add a dated column so history is kept and errors are caught.

modules.title: Advanced Drafting: Flat-Pattern Manipulation, Princess Lines, Sleeves and Collars
modules.overview: With a fitted block in hand, you can create almost any style on paper. This module teaches slash-and-spread and pivot methods for adding fullness, yokes and flare; drafting and truing princess-line panels; drafting set-in, puff and bishop sleeves that fit the armhole; and drafting stand, Peter Pan and shirt collars that sit neatly at the neck.

lessons.title: Flat-pattern manipulation: yokes, gathers, pleats and flare
objectives: Explain the difference between slash-and-spread and pivot methods
Separate a yoke from a block and transfer the dart into it
Add controlled fullness for gathers or pleats
Turn a straight skirt block into a flared skirt by closing darts

blocks.text: **Flat-pattern manipulation** means changing a tested block on paper to create a new style, without drafting from zero. Because the block already fits, every style made from it keeps the same fit at the important points: neck, shoulder, bust and waist. Two techniques do almost all the work.

blocks.title: Two ways to change a pattern
items: Slash and spread
Pivot
left: Cut lines on a copy of the block
Open the cuts to add width
right: Trace the block, then rotate it
No cutting of the master copy
blocks.caption: Both give the same result; choose the one that suits the change and your experience.

blocks.text: Always work on a **copy** of the block, never the master. Mark the grain line, bust point and notches on the copy before you start, so you can see how they move.
Separating a yoke

A yoke is a fitted section across the shoulders, chest or hips, joined to a looser lower part. On a bodice, a front yoke line can be drawn from the armhole to the centre front, passing near the tip of the shoulder dart. Cut along the yoke line. Then close the part of the dart that falls inside the yoke, and true the yoke seam. The yoke now fits the shoulders without a dart, because the dart has been absorbed into the seam.
Adding fullness for gathers and pleats

items: On the lower piece below the yoke, draw vertical slash lines about 3 to 5 cm apart, from the yoke edge to the hem.
Cut along each line from the top to the hem, leaving a tiny paper hinge at one end if you want fullness only at the top.
Spread each cut evenly on fresh paper. The total spread is the extra width you want gathered or pleated.
Tape down, redraw the yoke edge and hem as smooth curves, and mark the gathering zone between two notches.
For pleats, fold the paper along the pleat lines before cutting the top edge, so the edge is correct when the pleats are closed.

blocks.text: How much fullness? A common starting point for soft gathers is about one and a half times the finished length of the seam; for heavy gathers about two times. A fabric like chiffon gathers beautifully at two times, while a stiff aso-oke would look bulky. Test on a strip of your fabric before deciding.

blocks.name: creative-draft
blocks.alt: A designer drafting ideas on paper
blocks.caption: Flat-pattern manipulation turns one tested block into many styles on paper.

blocks.text: From straight skirt to flared skirt

Take the front skirt block with its waist dart. Draw a line from the dart point straight down to the hem, parallel to the grain. Cut up this line to the dart point. Close the dart at the waist; the slash opens at the hem. The dart width has become **flare at the hem**, and the waist still fits. For more flare, add further slash lines and spread them at the hem. A circle skirt is the extreme version of the same idea.

blocks.title: Worked example: a yoked peplum blouse with gathers
blocks.context: For example, Zainab in Abuja wants to make a yoked blouse with a gathered peplum from her tested bodice block for an ankara set. The front waist measures 20 cm on the quarter pattern.
steps: She draws a front yoke line 8 cm below the shoulder at the armhole, curving to 12 cm below the neck at centre front, and closes the shoulder dart into it.
She shortens the bodice to the natural waist and transfers the waist dart into a seam joining the peplum.
For the peplum, she wants 1.5 times fullness. The front waist seam is 20 cm on the quarter, so the peplum top edge needs 30 cm.
She draws a 20 cm by 15 cm rectangle, slashes it into five strips and spreads each gap by 2.5 cm at the top, giving 30 cm.
She marks notches at the side and centre front and tests the peplum in calico before cutting the ankara.
blocks.result: The blouse fits at the shoulders and waist because both come from the block, and the peplum has even, controlled fullness. Zainab saves the yoke and peplum pieces as a new style in her pattern register.

blocks.text: The pivot method gives the same results without cutting. To move a dart, trace the block from the centre front up to the first dart leg. Hold the paper down with an awl on the bust point, rotate the block until the dart leg closes onto the traced line, and trace the rest. The opening appears wherever you started tracing. Once you are confident, pivoting is faster and keeps your block copies intact, which matters when you work with expensive pattern card. Whichever method you use, label the new piece with its own style name and date, because a manipulated pattern is a new pattern.

blocks.title: True every new seam
blocks.text: After any manipulation, place the two seams that will be sewn together side by side and check they are the same length and meet at a smooth angle. This is called truing. Fix it on paper, never on fabric.

takeaways: Always manipulate a copy of the tested block
Slash-and-spread and pivot give the same result by different routes
Closing a dart can become a yoke seam, gathers or hem flare
Test fullness on your actual fabric and true every new seam

activity.title: Three styles from one block
steps: Make three copies of your bodice or skirt block at quarter or half scale.
On copy one, separate a yoke and close the dart into it.
On copy two, add 1.5 times gathering fullness below a yoke.
On copy three, close the skirt dart to create hem flare.
True each new seam and label every piece.
activity.evidence: Photo of the three manipulated patterns with labels and truing marks

lessons.title: Princess lines and panel seams: drafting, truing and shaping
objectives: Draft shoulder and armhole princess lines from a fitted bodice block
Add notches and true curved panel seams
Use panel seams to shape for a full bust and a curvy waist
Extend princess lines into a fitted gown or mermaid silhouette

blocks.text: A princess seam is a long curved seam that runs over the bust and down towards the hem. Unlike a dart, which is a fold that stops at a point, a princess seam is a full seam that divides the bodice into panels. It can start at the shoulder or at the armhole. Because the shaping is spread along the whole seam, princess lines can fit curvy bodies very closely, which is why they are common in fitted owambe gowns, corset dresses and mermaid styles.

blocks.title: Shoulder princess versus armhole princess
items: Shoulder princess
Armhole princess
blocks.caption: Both pass through or near the bust point; choose by style and fit need.

blocks.text: Drafting an armhole princess

items: Trace the front block with shoulder (or side) dart and waist dart, bust point marked.
Pivot or slash so the dart moves to the armhole: draw a curved line from about one third of the way up the front armhole to the bust point, cut it, close the original dart.
Join the armhole dart to the waist dart through the bust point with a smooth curve. This is the princess line.
Separate the centre front panel and the side front panel along the line, each keeping its own side of the dart.
Add notches: one about 6 to 8 cm above the bust point and one about 6 to 8 cm below, plus one at the waist.
True the seam: the two sides of a princess seam are different shapes but must be the same length between notches, or have a deliberate small ease over the bust.

blocks.title: Ease over the bust
blocks.text: On the side front panel, the curve over the bust is longer than the matching centre front edge. Some pattern makers keep a small amount of ease there (often a few millimetres) to shape over the bust; others make them exactly equal. Decide, then mark it between the bust notches so sewers ease it in evenly.

blocks.name: dress
blocks.caption: Princess panels shape a fitted gown over the bust and waist without visible darts.

blocks.text: Shaping complex figures with panels

Each princess seam is a place where you can add or remove width independently. On a full bust, you can add width to the side front panel at bust level and blend it back to nothing at the waist and armhole. On a client with a small waist and full hips, you can take in each seam at the waist and let it out at the hip. A gown with front and back princess seams plus side seams has **six to eight seams** where you can adjust, so the fit can follow almost any curve.

The rule is to **share the change**. If the gown needs to lose 4 cm at the waist, take a little from each seam rather than all from the side seams. Large changes in one seam distort the shape and pull the grain off.

blocks.title: Worked example: sharing a waist reduction across panels
blocks.context: For example, Efe in Benin City makes a mermaid gown in lace over a satin lining. At the toile fitting, the waist is 6 cm too big all round, while bust and hip are correct.
steps: The gown has front and back princess seams on both sides plus two side seams: six seams in total.
Each seam has two edges, giving twelve edges. 6 cm divided by 12 = 0.5 cm taken from each edge at the waist.
She marks 0.5 cm in at the waist notch on each panel edge and blends back to the original line about 10 cm above and below.
She re-trues each seam pair so lengths still match.
On the satin lining, she makes the same change so the lining and lace move together.
blocks.result: The waist is reduced evenly, the grain stays straight down each panel, and the lace motifs remain balanced. One large change at the side seams would have pulled the princess lines towards the sides.

blocks.text: Princess panels also make lace placement easier. Because each panel is cut separately, you can centre a large lace motif on the centre front panel and mirror motifs on the side panels, something impossible on a single-piece bodice. Lay each panel on the lace in a single layer, right side up, and turn the second side front panel over so the motifs mirror. Cut lining panels from the same pattern pieces so the lining follows exactly the same shaping.
Extending to the hem

For a fitted gown, extend the princess lines from the waist through the hip to the hem. For a mermaid or trumpet shape, decide the flare point, often around knee level, and add flare to each panel edge from that point to the hem. Add the same amount to both edges of each seam so panels stay balanced, and true the hem as one smooth curve when all panels are placed side by side.

takeaways: A princess seam is a full seam through or near the bust, not a fold
Notch above and below the bust and true each panel pair
Panels let you add or remove width independently on complex figures
Share large changes across all seams to keep the grain straight

activity.title: Draft and true a princess bodice
steps: Trace your front and back bodice blocks at half scale.
Draft an armhole princess on the front and a shoulder princess on the back.
Separate the panels, add notches, and true the seams.
Calculate how you would share a 4 cm waist reduction across all seam edges.
Mark the planned change on the panels in a different colour.

lessons.title: Drafting sleeves that fit the armhole: set-in, puff and bishop
objectives: Measure the front and back armhole on the bodice pattern
Draft a one-piece set-in sleeve with a cap that fits the armhole
Explain how cap height affects fit and movement
Turn the basic sleeve into puff and bishop sleeves

blocks.text: A beautifully fitted bodice is ruined by a sleeve that twists, pulls or will not go into the armhole. The secret is that **the sleeve is drafted from the armhole**, not only from the arm. The curve at the top of the sleeve, called the **sleeve cap** or sleeve head, must match the length of the armhole with a small, planned amount of extra length called cap ease.
Measurements you need

items: **Front armhole and back armhole lengths**, measured on the bodice pattern along the stitching line, with a tape on its edge or a flexible curve. Measure from shoulder point to side seam for each.
**Upper arm (bicep)** plus ease. For a fitted woven sleeve, a few centimetres of ease is usual; for a loose sleeve, much more.
**Sleeve length** from shoulder point to wrist, with the arm slightly bent.
**Wrist** or the desired sleeve opening for short or three-quarter sleeves.

blocks.text: Cap height decides fit and movement

The **cap height** is the distance from the top of the sleeve down to the bicep line. A **high cap** makes a narrow sleeve that hangs smoothly with the arm down, which looks elegant in a fitted gown but restricts lifting the arm. A **low cap** makes a wider sleeve with more movement, as in shirts, kaftans and workwear. Both sleeves can fit the same armhole: as the cap gets lower, the sleeve gets wider.

blocks.title: High cap versus low cap
items: High cap
Low cap
blocks.caption: Cap height trades a clean look against freedom of movement.

blocks.text: Drafting a basic set-in sleeve

items: Draw a vertical centre line equal to the sleeve length. The top point is the crown.
Choose a cap height and square a bicep line across at that depth.

From the crown, draw a straight line down to the bicep line on the back side, equal to the back armhole length. Repeat on the front side with the front armhole length. Where they meet the bicep line sets the sleeve width.
Check the bicep width against her upper arm plus ease. If it is too narrow, lower the cap height slightly and redraw; if too wide, raise it.
Divide each diagonal into parts and draw the cap curve: outward above the line near the crown, inward below it near the underarm, with the front scooped a little more than the back.
Draw the underarm seams down to the wrist width, mark one notch at the front and two at the back, and mark the crown notch to match the shoulder seam.

blocks.text: Measure the finished cap curve. It should be longer than the armhole by the cap ease you want. For a fitted blouse in medium-weight woven fabric, many pattern makers aim for roughly 2 to 4 cm; shirts and knit tops need little or none; heavy fabrics take less because they do not ease well. If the curve is too long, flatten the cap slightly; if too short, add a little height or curve.

blocks.title: Worked example: checking cap ease
blocks.context: For example, Adaeze in Owerri drafts a sleeve for a fitted crepe dress. On her bodice, the front armhole measures 22 cm and the back 23.5 cm. Her client's bicep is 32 cm.
steps: Total armhole = 22 + 23.5 = 45.5 cm.
She wants about 3 cm of cap ease for crepe, so the cap curve should be about 48.5 cm.
With her first cap height, the bicep width comes out at 31 cm, less than the 32 cm arm. She lowers the cap height by 1 cm and redraws; the bicep is now about 34 cm, giving 2 cm ease.
She measures the new cap curve: 49.5 cm, which is 4 cm over the armhole. She flattens the curve slightly near the crown and remeasures: 48.6 cm.
She sews a calico test sleeve into the toile and checks it hangs without twisting.
blocks.result: The sleeve eases smoothly into the armhole with no puckers, and the client can lift her arm comfortably. Adaeze writes the cap height and ease on the sleeve pattern for future use.

blocks.name: womans-clothes
blocks.caption: A well-drafted sleeve cap is the difference between a homemade and a professional blouse.

blocks.text: Puff and bishop sleeves

items: **Puff sleeve**: slash the cap from crown to bicep in several lines and spread at the top only. Raise the crown by a few centimetres so the fullness stands up. Gather the extra into the armhole between the notches.
**Bishop sleeve**: slash from wrist up to the cap and spread at the bottom, adding length at the back of the wrist so it blouses over a cuff. Gather into a cuff or elastic.
**Both**: keep the armhole notches and underarm curve unchanged so the sleeve still fits the bodice.

blocks.title: Sew the sleeve test first
blocks.text: Sleeves are cheap to test and expensive to get wrong in lace. Always sew one sleeve in calico into the toile armhole before cutting the real fabric.

takeaways: Draft the sleeve from the armhole lengths, not only the arm
Cap height trades a smooth look for freedom of movement
Measure the cap curve and set a planned cap ease
Puff and bishop sleeves come from slashing the basic sleeve

activity.title: Draft and test a set-in sleeve
steps: Measure front and back armholes on your bodice block.
Draft a set-in sleeve and record cap height, bicep width and cap ease.
Sew it in calico into a bodice toile and photograph the arm down and arm lifted.
Make one puff variation on paper from the same sleeve.
Write what you would change after the test.
activity.evidence: Sleeve pattern with measurements written on it, plus photos of the calico test

lessons.title: Drafting collars: mandarin stand, Peter Pan and shirt collar with stand
objectives: Measure the neckline on the pattern for collar drafting
Draft a mandarin stand collar and explain how curving it changes the fit
Draft a Peter Pan collar from the bodice neckline
Draft a two-piece shirt collar with a separate stand

blocks.text: Collars sit at the most visible part of a garment, right next to the face. A collar that stands away from the neck, twists at the front or shows its seam ruins the whole look. Every collar is drafted from one key number: the **neckline length** of the pattern, measured on the stitching line from centre back to centre front. Measure the back neck and front neck separately, because collar notches must line up with the shoulder seam.

blocks.title: Collar drafting sequence
items: Finalise bodice neckline
Measure back and front neck
Draft collar shape
True and notch
Test in calico
blocks.caption: Never draft a collar before the neckline has been fitted, or the collar will not match.

blocks.text: Mandarin or stand collar

The stand collar is a narrow band that stands up around the neck. It is used on kaftans, senator-style tops and many blouses. Start with a rectangle: length equals half the neckline (centre back to centre front), height equals the stand height you want, often 3 to 4 cm. A straight rectangle stands away from the neck. To make it hug the neck, **raise the front end** of the lower edge by about 1 to 1.5 cm and draw a smooth curve from the centre back to the raised point, then curve the top edge parallel. The more you curve it upward, the closer it sits to the neck.

blocks.name: kimono
blocks.alt: A robe with a neat neckline
blocks.caption: Stand collars and neat neck finishes are common on kaftans and robe-style garments.

blocks.text: Peter Pan collar

A Peter Pan collar lies flat on the shoulders with rounded ends. It is drafted directly from the bodice. Place the front and back bodice patterns together at the neck point of the shoulder seam. Overlap the shoulders at the armhole end by about 1 to 2 cm. This overlap shortens the outer edge slightly, which gives the collar a small roll so the seam hides under it. Trace the neckline, then draw the outer edge parallel at the collar width you want, often 6 to 8 cm, rounding the front.

items: **No overlap**: collar lies completely flat, and the neck seam may show.
**1 to 2 cm overlap**: slight roll, seam hidden, the usual choice.
**Large overlap**: more roll and stand, moving towards a different collar style.

blocks.text: Shirt collar with separate stand

items: Draft the stand like a curved mandarin collar, adding the button extension at the front end (equal to the button stand width on the shirt front).
Draw the collar on top of the stand: its lower edge follows the top edge of the stand but curves **downward** at the front, the opposite direction to the stand.
Make the collar slightly deeper than the stand at the back, often 1 to 1.5 cm more, so it covers the stand seam when it folds over.
Draw the collar point shape at the front, with the point length and spread to suit the style.
Add notches at centre back and at the shoulder position on both stand and collar.
Cut the under collar slightly smaller than the upper collar at the outer edge, a few millimetres, so the seam rolls to the underside.

blocks.title: Worked example: a stand collar for a kaftan
blocks.context: For example, Aisha, a tailor in Sokoto, is drafting a stand collar for a man's kaftan. On the pattern, the back neck is 8.5 cm and the front neck 12 cm, centre back to centre front.
steps: Half neckline = 8.5 + 12 = 20.5 cm. She draws a rectangle 20.5 cm long and 3.5 cm high, plus a 1.5 cm button overlap at the front.
She marks a shoulder notch 8.5 cm from centre back.
She raises the front end of the lower edge by 1.2 cm and draws a smooth curve from centre back, then curves the top edge parallel.
She cuts the collar on grain, interfaces one layer with woven fusible, and tests it on the calico toile.
The collar sits close at the back but slightly away at the front, so she raises the front another 0.5 cm and retests.
blocks.result: The final collar sits evenly around the neck with the shoulder notch matching the shoulder seam. Aisha writes the curve amount on the pattern so every kaftan in that size gets the same collar.

blocks.title: Stretching necklines
blocks.text: Curved necklines are partly on the bias and stretch easily while you handle them. Staystitch the bodice neckline just inside the seam line immediately after cutting, so it keeps the length your collar was drafted to fit.
Keep a set of collar patterns for each neckline in your block range. Once a collar works on a tested neckline, it works on every style made from that block.

takeaways: Every collar starts from the measured neckline on the pattern
Curving a stand collar upward makes it hug the neck
Overlapping shoulders when drafting a Peter Pan collar creates roll
A shirt collar curves downward at the front while its stand curves upward

activity.title: Collar sampler
steps: Measure the back and front neckline on your bodice block.
Draft a mandarin collar, a Peter Pan collar and a shirt collar with stand.
Cut each in calico and interface one layer.
Pin each to a bodice toile and photograph how it sits from the front and side.
Note one adjustment for each collar.
