quiz.q: Halima closes the waist dart on a straight skirt front after slashing from dart point to hem. What happens?
options: The dart width becomes flare at the hem while the waist still fits
quiz.explain: Closing the dart opens the slash at the hem, turning the dart volume into hem flare without changing the waist fit.

quiz.q: A peplum joins a waist seam of 24 cm on the quarter pattern. For 1.5 times fullness, how long should the peplum top edge be?
quiz.explain: 24 cm times 1.5 = 36 cm.

quiz.q: A gown with six seams (twelve edges) must lose 6 cm at the waist. How much should come off each edge if shared evenly?
quiz.explain: 6 cm divided by 12 edges = 0.5 cm per edge. Sharing keeps the grain straight and panels balanced.

quiz.q: A client says her new sleeves look elegant but she cannot lift her arms to dance. What change helps most?
options: Lower the sleeve cap, which widens the sleeve and frees movement
quiz.explain: A high cap gives a narrow, restrictive sleeve. Lowering the cap widens the sleeve and gives more movement.

quiz.q: Front armhole 21 cm, back armhole 22.5 cm, and you want 3 cm cap ease. What should the sleeve cap curve measure?
quiz.explain: 21 + 22.5 = 43.5 cm armhole, plus 3 cm ease = 46.5 cm.

quiz.q: A straight rectangle stand collar stands away from the neck at the front. What should the tailor do?
options: Raise the front end of the lower edge and curve it
quiz.explain: Curving the stand upward at the front makes the collar hug the neck.

quiz.q: Why overlap the shoulders by 1 to 2 cm when drafting a Peter Pan collar?
options: To give a slight roll that hides the neck seam
quiz.explain: The overlap shortens the outer edge so the collar rolls slightly and covers the seam.

modules.title: African Silhouettes, Production Patterns and Grading
modules.overview: This module applies your drafting skills to garments your clients wear every week: the Yoruba iro and buba, and the West African kaftan and boubou. You then learn to turn a single tested pattern into a production pattern set with markers that save fabric, and to grade it across a full size range using grade rules.

lessons.title: Drafting iro and buba: kimono-cut blouse, gussets and tailored wrapper
objectives: Describe the parts of an iro and buba outfit and how each is worn
Draft a kimono-cut buba from measurements, with a neckline facing
Add an underarm gusset to give movement to a close kimono sleeve
Convert a traditional wrapper into a tailored ready-to-wear iro

blocks.text: Iro and buba is a Yoruba women's outfit. The **buba** is a loose blouse, the **iro** is a wrapper tied around the waist, and the outfit is commonly completed with a **gele** (head tie) and sometimes an **ipele** or **iborun** worn over the shoulder. Fabrics range from ankara to lace and the hand-woven **aso-oke**. Because the buba is loose, many tailors think it needs no skill. At advanced level, a buba that hangs evenly, does not pull at the underarm and has a crisp neckline is a mark of quality.

blocks.name: womans-clothes
blocks.caption: The buba is loose, but a professional one still hangs evenly and moves freely.

blocks.text: The kimono-cut buba

Many bubas are **kimono-cut**: the sleeve is cut in one piece with the body, with no armhole seam. This saves time and suits wide, flowing sleeves. The pattern is a T-shape folded at the shoulder line.

items: Measure bust, hip, shoulder to desired length (often hip length or longer), and the sleeve length from the neck point over the shoulder to the desired sleeve end.
Decide the ease. A relaxed buba often has 20 cm or more of ease at the bust; a more fitted modern buba less. Write your choice.
Draw a centre line for the length. Square across at the shoulder line. Mark the half width at bust level: (bust plus ease) divided by 4 for each quarter.
From the neck point, draw the sleeve along the shoulder line, sloping down slightly (a few centimetres over the sleeve length) so the sleeve does not stand up stiffly.
Draw the underarm curve from the sleeve end down to the side seam. A deep curve gives a batwing look; a shallow, higher curve gives a closer sleeve.
Draw the neckline: front deeper than back. Add a facing pattern 5 to 6 cm wide that follows the neckline.

blocks.title: Kimono-cut versus set-in buba sleeve
items: Kimono-cut sleeve
Set-in sleeve
blocks.caption: Choose by style: flowing tradition or a closer modern fit.

blocks.text: Underarm gussets

When a kimono sleeve is made closer to the body, lifting the arm pulls the whole garment up and can tear the underarm seam. A **gusset** solves this: a small diamond or triangle of fabric set into a slash at the underarm. It adds length exactly where the arm needs to move. Cut gussets on the bias for extra give, and reinforce the slash point with a small piece of fusible interfacing before cutting into it.

blocks.title: Aso-oke and sleeves
blocks.text: Aso-oke is woven in narrow strips joined together and can be stiff. Plan where the strip joins fall before cutting, so they run straight and symmetrically, and avoid deep, curved underarms that the stiff fabric resists.
From wrapper to tailored iro

The traditional iro is a rectangle of fabric wrapped and tucked at the waist. Many clients now ask for a **ready-to-wear iro** that stays in place. Common methods include adding a waistband with hooks or ties, sewing in an elasticated back section, or shaping it as a wrap skirt with a fixed inner panel. Measure the waist and hip, and decide the overlap at the front (enough that it does not open when walking). Keep the outer layer long and draped so it still looks like a wrapper.

Finish the buba neckline with care, because it frames the face and the gele. Staystitch the neckline after cutting, interface the facing lightly, understitch the facing to the seam allowance so it rolls inside, and press over a tailor's ham. For lace bubas, a narrow bias binding in a matching lining fabric often looks cleaner than a wide facing that shows through the lace.

blocks.title: Worked example: drafting a set of buba and tailored iro
blocks.context: For example, Yetunde in Abeokuta drafts a buba and tailored iro for a client with bust 104 cm, hip 112 cm, waist 90 cm. The client wants a kimono sleeve to the elbow and wants the iro to stay in place for dancing.
steps: She chooses 20 cm bust ease: (104 + 20) divided by 4 = 31 cm for each quarter at bust level.
Hip check: she needs at least (112 + 8) divided by 4 = 30 cm at hip level for comfort. Her 31 cm side line is enough, so the side seam can run straight.
Because the client wants a closer sleeve, she adds a bias-cut gusset of 10 cm by 10 cm at each underarm.
For the iro, she adds a 4 cm waistband sized to 90 cm plus 2 cm ease, with a 25 cm front overlap and two hooks and bars.
She tests the buba in calico and asks the client to lift both arms and dance a few steps.
blocks.result: The buba hangs evenly and does not lift when the client raises her arms, and the iro stays secure while looking like a traditional wrapper. Yetunde saves both as a style in her pattern register.

takeaways: Iro and buba combine a loose blouse, a wrapper, gele and sometimes ipele
A kimono-cut buba is a T-shape; ease and underarm curve set the look
Bias-cut gussets free movement in closer kimono sleeves
A tailored iro adds a waistband, ties or a fixed panel but keeps the draped look

activity.title: Draft a buba and iro
steps: Take bust, hip, waist and length measurements from one client or family member.
Choose your ease and draft a kimono-cut buba at half scale or full size.
Add a neckline facing pattern and a gusset pattern.
Draft a tailored iro with waistband and overlap.
Write the ease and overlap you used on the patterns.
activity.evidence: Photos of the buba, facing, gusset and iro patterns with measurements written on them

lessons.title: Drafting kaftans and boubous: wide robes, fabric width and embroidered necklines
objectives: Describe the boubou and its regional names and variations
Draft a boubou from arm span, length and fabric width
Plan side panels or gores when the fabric is too narrow
Draft a neckline and placket that support embroidery

blocks.text: The **boubou** is a flowing, wide-sleeved robe worn across West Africa. It is known by many names, including **babban riga** in Hausa, **mboubou** in Wolof and **grand boubou** in French-speaking countries. The grand boubou is the formal version, often richly embroidered and worn over a caftan and loose trousers. Boubous are often made from cotton damask called **bazin**, or other cotton fabrics. A **kaftan** in Nigerian usage is usually a long tunic, narrower than a boubou, often with a stand collar or embroidered neckline, worn by men and women.

blocks.name: kimono
blocks.caption: Wide robes are drafted mostly from rectangles, so fabric width and neckline work matter most.

blocks.text: The rectangle principle

A traditional boubou is built from large rectangles. The main piece is folded at the shoulder line, so the front and back are one piece with a neck opening cut in the middle. The width usually spans from wrist to wrist with the arms held out, which forms the sleeves. Side seams are sewn from the hem up to the underarm, leaving the sleeve openings free. Because the shape is simple, the quality is in the proportions, the neckline and the finishing.

items: Measure arm span from wrist to wrist with arms held out, and shoulder to ankle (or desired length).
Main piece: width = arm span (or the sleeve width the style needs); length = 2 times the garment length, folded at the shoulder.
Mark the centre point of the fold. This is the centre of the neckline.
Mark side seams: from the hem up to the underarm point, leaving the sleeve opening (for example 30 to 40 cm from the fold).
Draw the neckline: a round or boat neck, with a front slit if needed for the head to pass through. Draft a facing that follows it.

blocks.title: Boubou drafting order
items: Measure span and length
Check fabric width
Plan panels if needed
Draft neckline and facing
Mark embroidery area
blocks.caption: Check fabric width before drawing anything, because it decides the construction.

blocks.text: When the fabric is too narrow

Many fabrics are narrower than an adult's arm span. For example, ankara is often about 115 to 120 cm wide (check yours), while an arm span may be 160 cm or more. The solution is to **add side panels**: the centre panel uses the full fabric width, and two side panels are joined to make up the total. Place the seams symmetrically, and match the print where they join. In some traditional garments, extra triangular pieces (gores) are set into the sides to add swing at the hem.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning fabric for a woman's boubou
blocks.context: For example, Hadiza in Kano is making a woman's boubou. Arm span 158 cm, shoulder to ankle 138 cm. The fabric is 116 cm wide.
steps: Main piece needs to be 158 cm wide, but the fabric is only 116 cm. Shortfall = 158 minus 116 = 42 cm.
She adds two side panels, each 21 cm finished plus 1.5 cm seam allowance on each side: 24 cm wide each.
Centre panel length = 2 times 138 = 276 cm, plus 3 cm hem allowance on each end: 282 cm.
Each side panel also runs the full folded length, 282 cm. Two side panels of 24 cm fit side by side in one 116 cm width, so they need one more 282 cm length.
Total fabric: 282 + 282 = 564 cm, about 5.64 m, plus allowance for the neckline facing and print matching. 6 yards is only about 5.49 m, which is not enough, so she buys 7 yards (about 6.4 m).
blocks.result: Hadiza calculates before she buys, finds that a standard 6 yards would be short, and buys 7. One yard is 0.9144 m, so always convert carefully when fabric is sold in yards.

blocks.text: Necklines that carry embroidery

The neckline is the showpiece of a kaftan or boubou. Draft the neckline and the embroidery area together. Mark a clear rectangle or shield shape around the neck and down the front where the embroidery will go, and keep seams out of it. Interface the embroidery area with a stable woven or tear-away stabiliser so stitches do not pucker the fabric. If you send pieces to a machine embroiderer, send the cut panel with the neckline traced but **not cut**, plus a paper template of the design area, so the embroidery is placed exactly. Cut the neckline after embroidery, then face it.

For a men's grand boubou set, the robe is only one of three garments: the inner caftan and the trousers are drafted separately from their own measurements. Draft the inner caftan first, because the boubou must slip over it comfortably, and check the boubou neckline against the caftan collar so the two sit well together.

blocks.title: Respect the style's origin
blocks.text: Boubou and kaftan styles differ by region and community, and some details have meaning. When a client asks for a specific traditional style, ask her to show you an example and confirm the details rather than guessing.

takeaways: A boubou is built from rectangles folded at the shoulder
Check fabric width first; add symmetrical side panels if it is too narrow
Convert yards to metres carefully: one yard is 0.9144 m
Embroider before cutting the neckline, then face it

activity.title: Boubou plan and fabric calculation
steps: Measure arm span and shoulder to ankle on one adult.
Choose a fabric width you can buy locally and calculate whether side panels are needed.
Draw the cutting plan with all pieces, seam allowances and hem allowances.
Calculate total fabric in metres and in yards.
Draft a neckline, facing and embroidery area template.
activity.evidence: Cutting plan with fabric calculation and the neckline and embroidery template

lessons.title: Production patterns, markers and cutting multiple layers
objectives: Convert a tested pattern into a complete production pattern set
Make a marker and calculate marker efficiency
Plan a lay for cutting several garments at once
Use a cutting ticket to control an order of many pieces

blocks.text: A bespoke pattern is used once or twice. A **production pattern** is used dozens or hundreds of times, often by someone other than you. It must be complete, durable and impossible to misread. This lesson shows how to move from one good toile to a pattern set that can cut thirty aso-ebi gowns or a boutique order without mistakes.
What a production pattern set includes

items: **Every piece**, including facings, interfacing, linings, pockets, gussets and waistbands, each as its own piece. Nothing is "cut by eye".
**Seam allowances included** and stated, often a consistent width such as 1 cm or 1.5 cm on most seams so sewers do not have to think.
**Notches, drill holes and grain lines** on every piece, as in Module 1.
**A pattern plan or header card** listing all pieces, cut quantities, fabric, trims and the date of the last revision.
**Card, not paper**, for any pattern you will use more than a few times. Hang the full set on one hook.

blocks.name: factory
blocks.caption: Production patterns let several people cut and sew the same style with the same result.

blocks.text: Markers and marker efficiency

A **marker** is the layout plan of all pattern pieces on the fabric, drawn on paper the width of the fabric. You arrange the pieces to use as little fabric as possible while keeping every grain line correct. Big pieces go down first, small pieces fill the gaps. When you find a good layout, trace it onto marker paper so you can reuse it.

**Marker efficiency** tells you how much of the fabric becomes garment and how much becomes waste. Efficiency percent = total area of pattern pieces divided by marker area (length times width), times 100. You can estimate pattern area by measuring each piece roughly as rectangles and triangles. Higher efficiency means lower fabric cost per garment.

blocks.title: Worked example: two markers for the same skirt
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat in Ilorin cuts flared skirts for a church choir order. Her pattern pieces total about 1.5 square metres per skirt. Fabric width is 1.5 m.
steps: Marker A, one skirt at a time: marker length 1.4 m. Area = 1.4 times 1.5 = 2.1 square metres. Efficiency = 1.5 divided by 2.1 times 100, about 71 percent.

Marker B, two skirts nested together, with one set of pieces turned to fit into the curves of the other: length 2.4 m. Area = 2.4 times 1.5 = 3.6 square metres. Pattern area = 3.0. Efficiency = 3.0 divided by 3.6 times 100, about 83 percent.
Fabric per skirt: Marker A uses 1.4 m, Marker B uses 1.2 m.
For 20 skirts, Marker B saves 20 times 0.2 = 4 m of fabric.
She checks that turning pieces is allowed: the fabric is a plain solid with no nap, so it is.
blocks.result: By nesting two sizes or two copies in one marker, Rukayat saves 4 m on the order. For a one-way print or velvet she would not turn pieces, and would accept a lower efficiency.

blocks.title: From tested pattern to cut bundles
items: Tested pattern
Production pattern set
Marker
Lay and cut
Bundles with tickets
blocks.caption: Each step adds control so many garments come out identical.

blocks.text: Lays and multi-layer cutting

A **lay** is several layers of fabric spread on top of each other so you can cut many garments at once. Spread each layer flat and smooth, with selvedges lined up on one side and grain straight. Do not stretch the fabric as you spread. Place the marker on top, weight it or pin through all layers outside the pieces, and cut with long sharp shears or a rotary cutter, keeping the blade upright. Too many layers make lower pieces bigger than upper ones because the blade drifts, so start with a small number of layers and check pieces from the top and bottom of the lay against the pattern.

blocks.title: Cutting tools
blocks.text: Rotary cutters and electric cloth cutters are very sharp. Always close or guard the blade when you put it down, cut away from your body, and keep the other hand flat and well away from the cutting line. Never leave blades where children can reach them.

For lace and other fabrics where motif placement matters, multi-layer cutting is often not possible. Cut these in a single layer, piece by piece, and accept the extra time in your price. Mixed orders, such as aso-ebi where each guest brings her own fabric, also need single cutting, but you can still use the same production pattern set and the same cutting ticket system.
Cutting tickets

For every order, write a **cutting ticket**: style, sizes and quantities, fabric and colour, number of layers, marker used, date and who cut it. After cutting, count the pieces against the ticket before bundling. The ticket follows the bundle through sewing and inspection, so you always know where each garment is.

takeaways: A production pattern set includes every piece, with allowances and full labels
Marker efficiency = pattern area divided by marker area, times 100
Nesting pieces saves fabric if the fabric has no nap or one-way print
Check top and bottom pieces of a lay, and track orders with cutting tickets

activity.title: Make and measure a marker
steps: Choose one pattern you have tested and complete every missing piece and label.
Make two different markers for it on paper the width of your usual fabric.
Estimate pattern area and calculate efficiency for both.
Write a cutting ticket for an imaginary order of ten pieces.
Note which marker you would use and why.

lessons.title: Grading across a full size range with grade rules
objectives: Explain grade points, grade rules and the base size
Write a simple grade rule table from a size chart
Move grade points to create the next size and nest the sizes
Grade a sleeve so it still fits the graded armhole

blocks.text: **Grading** is making a pattern bigger or smaller to fit a range of sizes while keeping the same style and proportions. In professional grading, you do not simply enlarge the whole pattern like a photocopy. You move specific points by planned amounts, because bodies do not grow evenly: a size larger is wider at the bust and hip, but the neck and shoulder grow only a little.

blocks.name: smart-resize
blocks.caption: Grading resizes a pattern by moving key points, not by enlarging everything equally.

blocks.text: Key terms

items: **Base size**: the size you drafted and fitted, usually the middle of your range.
**Grade points** (also called cardinal points): corners and key positions on the pattern that move, such as neck point, shoulder point, underarm, waist at side seam and hem at side seam.
**Grade rule**: how far each grade point moves, written as a horizontal movement (x) and a vertical movement (y) between neighbouring sizes.
**Nest**: all graded sizes drawn on top of each other from the same reference point. A good nest shows evenly spaced, parallel lines.

blocks.text: From size chart to grade rules

Start from the size chart you built in Module 2. If your bust interval is 5 cm, each quarter pattern (front or back half of one side) must grow by 5 divided by 4 = 1.25 cm in width at bust level. That width is shared among points: some at the side seam, some at the shoulder and neck. Lengths also grow, but by smaller amounts, and you decide them from your length data.

blocks.title: These numbers are an example
blocks.text: The table is an illustration of how a grade rule table looks for a 5 cm bust interval, measured from centre front at the waist as the fixed reference. Your own rules must come from your size chart and be tested by sewing the smallest and largest sizes.

blocks.title: Grading one size up
items: Fix reference point
Read grade rule
Move each grade point
Redraw lines and curves
Check seams match
blocks.caption: Repeat for each size, then nest all sizes to check the spacing.

blocks.text: Moving the points

items: Trace the base size on a large sheet. Choose a fixed reference, for example centre front at waist, and keep it in the same place for every size.
For each grade point, measure the x movement outward (or inward for smaller) and the y movement upward or downward, and mark the new point.
Redraw the lines between new points using the same curves as the base, shifted. Keep the armhole and neckline shapes parallel to the original.
Move notches and drill holes with the nearest grade point.
Repeat for every size and every piece, then check that seams that sew together are still the same length in each size.

blocks.text: Grading the sleeve to match

When the bodice armhole grows, the sleeve cap must grow to match, or the sleeve will not fit. Measure the graded armhole in each size and grade the sleeve so its cap length grows by the same amount, keeping the same cap ease you chose in Module 3. Grow the bicep width in step with your upper arm data. Sew-test the sleeve in the largest size, where problems show most.

blocks.title: Worked example: grading a buba from M to XL
blocks.context: For example, Tola from Module 2 uses her size chart with a 5 cm bust interval to grade her buba pattern, base size M, up to L and XL.
steps: Quarter pattern width grows 1.25 cm per size at the bust. From M to XL is two sizes, so the side seam moves 2.5 cm outward in total.
She chooses a length grade of 1 cm per size, so XL is 2 cm longer than M at the hem.
Because the buba is kimono-cut, she moves the sleeve end outward by her sleeve length grade of 0.5 cm per size and keeps the underarm curve shape parallel.
She nests M, L and XL and checks that the lines are evenly spaced.
She sews the XL in calico on a willing XL client before cutting the production order.
blocks.result: The three sizes have the same style and proportions, and the XL test confirms the grade. She can now cut a mixed size order from one marker.

blocks.text: As your size range grows, free open-source pattern software such as Seamly2D lets you build patterns from measurement formulas, so new sizes are generated from a size chart. It does not replace understanding: you still need to know which points should move and by how much.

takeaways: Grading moves grade points by planned x and y amounts
Grade rules come from your size chart intervals
Keep a fixed reference point and nest sizes to check spacing
Grade the sleeve cap to match the graded armhole and test the largest size

activity.title: Grade one pattern three sizes
steps: Write a grade rule table for one bodice or buba pattern from your size chart.
Grade the pattern one size up and one size down from the base.
Nest the three sizes on one sheet with a fixed reference point.
Check matching seams and the armhole and sleeve lengths in each size.
Sew-test the largest size in calico.
activity.evidence: Grade rule table, photo of the nested sizes and a photo of the largest size test

quiz.q: A client wants a closer kimono-cut buba sleeve, but the underarm pulls when she lifts her arm. What is the professional fix?
options: Set a bias-cut gusset into the underarm
quiz.explain: A gusset adds length at the underarm where the arm needs to move, without making the whole garment loose.

quiz.q: A boubou needs to be 160 cm wide and the fabric is 115 cm wide. How much width must side panels add in total (before seam allowances)?
quiz.explain: 160 minus 115 = 45 cm, shared between two symmetrical side panels.

quiz.q: When should the neckline of an embroidered kaftan be cut?
options: Before embroidery, so the embroiderer can see it
After embroidery, using a traced line and template to place the design
Only after the garment is fully sewn
quiz.explain: Tracing but not cutting keeps the fabric stable during embroidery. Cut the neckline after, then face it.

quiz.q: Pattern pieces total 2.4 square metres and the marker is 2 m long on 1.5 m fabric. What is the marker efficiency?
quiz.explain: Marker area = 2 times 1.5 = 3 square metres. 2.4 divided by 3 times 100 = 80 percent.

quiz.q: Why should you not turn pattern pieces upside down in a marker for velvet?
options: Velvet has a nap, so pieces would look different in colour or sheen
quiz.explain: Pile fabrics like velvet need a with-nap layout, with all pieces facing the same way.

quiz.q: With a 5 cm bust interval between sizes, how much does each quarter pattern grow at the bust?
quiz.explain: 5 cm divided by 4 quarters = 1.25 cm per quarter pattern.

quiz.q: After grading a bodice up two sizes, the sleeve will not fit the armhole. What was missed?
options: The sleeve cap was not graded to match the graded armhole
The grain line was not moved
The neckline facing was not graded
quiz.explain: The sleeve cap must grow with the armhole while keeping the same cap ease.

modules.title: Fitting Complex Bodies, Quality Control and Professional Client Work
modules.overview: The final module brings everything together at the level clients pay most for. You will run structured toile fittings, read drag lines to diagnose fit problems, make full bust, sway back, shoulder and arm alterations on the pattern, run a quality control system for single garments and production orders, and manage high-value clients and pricing professionally.

lessons.title: Running a toile fitting and reading drag lines
objectives: Prepare a toile that gives reliable fitting information
Run a fitting in a fixed order from top to bottom
Read drag lines and folds to find the cause of a fit problem
Record fitting changes clearly on the toile and the order card

blocks.text: A **toile** (also called a muslin) is a test garment sewn from cheap fabric such as calico, close in weight to the final fabric. For complex bodies and expensive fabrics, the toile is where the real fitting happens. A good fitting is calm, structured and quick, and it gives you clear marks to take back to the pattern.
Preparing the toile

items: Cut from the pattern with all markings: centre front, centre back, bust points, waist line, hip line and grain lines drawn on the calico with a marker.
Sew with a long machine stitch so seams are easy to open, and sew seam allowances to the outside on one side if you want to pin changes easily.
Include one sleeve and the collar if the final garment has them.
Choose a calico of similar weight to the final fabric: a light calico for chiffon gowns, a heavier one for aso-oke or brocade.

blocks.name: fitting-piece
blocks.alt: A person fitting a piece into place
blocks.caption: A toile is where each piece of the fit puzzle is checked before the real fabric is cut.

blocks.text: Fitting in a fixed order

Work from the top down, because changes at the shoulder affect everything below. Check the shoulders and neck first, then the bust, armhole and back, then the waist, then hips and hem, and finally the sleeve and collar. Fix the biggest problem first: a shoulder that is too wide can cause folds lower down that disappear once the shoulder is corrected.

blocks.title: Toile fitting order
items: Shoulders and neck
Bust and armhole
Back and waist
Hips and hem
Sleeve and collar
blocks.caption: Fit from the top down; a correction above often removes problems below.

blocks.text: Reading drag lines

**Drag lines** are diagonal or horizontal wrinkles caused by fabric pulling or collecting. The key rule: **drag lines point towards the problem**. Tight areas create pulling lines that radiate from the tight spot. Loose areas create soft folds that hang. Look at where the lines start and where they point.

head: What you see
Likely cause
Typical fix
rows: Diagonal pulls from the bust towards the side seam and armhole
Not enough room over the bust
Horizontal folds just above the back waist
Back too long for a sway back
Fold out a wedge at centre back waist
Diagonal folds from neck towards the armhole
Shoulders more sloping than the pattern
Pulling across the upper back when arms move forward
Add width at the back armhole area
Sleeve twists or pulls across the upper arm
Bicep too narrow or cap misaligned
Widen the sleeve, check the crown notch
Extra length in the armhole, often with a full bust
Small armhole dart transferred away, or a bust adjustment

blocks.title: Ask her to move
blocks.text: Before you finish, ask the client to sit, raise her arms, reach forward and walk a few steps. Many fit problems only appear in movement, and owambe gowns must survive dancing.

Keep the fitting professional and private. Fit in a screened corner or a separate room, with a mirror the client can see. Explain what you are checking as you go, ask before touching near the bust or hips, and keep pins pointing away from her skin. If the client is uncomfortable with you pinning close to the body, ask her to hold a section while you mark it, or have a female assistant present. Clients who feel safe and respected at fittings become your most loyal clients.
Marking and recording

Pin changes symmetrically unless the body is asymmetric. Mark new seam lines on the calico with a marker in a different colour, and write the amount beside each change, for example "take in 1 cm" or "add 2 cm". Take photos from front, side and back with consent. Before the client leaves, transfer each change to her order card. Do not trust memory after a busy day.

blocks.title: Worked example: diagnosing a toile in order
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Calabar fits a toile for a fitted lace sheath gown. She notices diagonal folds from the neck towards the armhole, pulls from the bust to the side seams, and horizontal folds above the back waist.
steps: She starts at the top. Unpinning the shoulder seam and re-pinning it 1 cm lower at the shoulder point removes the neck-to-armhole folds.
With shoulders fixed, the bust pulls are still there. She unpicks the side seam at bust level and the toile springs open by about 2 cm on each side: she notes "FBA about 2 cm each side".
At the back she pinches out a horizontal fold of about 1.5 cm at the centre back waist, tapering to nothing at the side seam.
She asks the client to sit and raise her arms. Everything holds.
She writes all three changes on the toile and the order card and photographs the marked toile.
blocks.result: Grace leaves the fitting with three clear pattern changes, each with an amount. Fixing in order stopped her from chasing folds that were really caused by the shoulder.

takeaways: A toile in similar-weight calico gives reliable fitting information
Fit from the top down and fix the biggest problem first
Drag lines point towards the problem
Mark amounts on the toile and record them before the client leaves

activity.title: Run a toile fitting
steps: Sew a bodice toile with all markings drawn on.
Fit it on a willing adult in the fixed order from top to bottom.
Photograph any drag lines and write the cause and fix for each.
Mark every change with its amount on the toile.
Transfer the changes to a fitting record.
activity.evidence: Photos of the marked toile and the completed fitting record

lessons.title: Pattern alterations for complex bodies: full bust, sway back, shoulders and arms
objectives: Perform a full bust adjustment on a darted bodice and on a princess pattern
Correct a sway back on the pattern
Adjust for sloping or square shoulders without changing armhole size
Widen a sleeve for a fuller upper arm

blocks.text: The toile tells you what is wrong. The pattern is where you fix it permanently. This lesson covers the four alterations you will make most often for real clients. Each one adds or removes length or width only where the body needs it, so the rest of the pattern stays balanced. Always alter a copy and keep the original.
Full bust adjustment (FBA) on a darted bodice

items: Mark the bust point. Draw line 1 from the bust point straight down to the waist, parallel to the grain. Draw line 2 from the bust point up to about one third of the way up the armhole. Draw line 3 through the middle of the side dart to the bust point.
Cut line 1 up to the bust point and continue along line 2 to the armhole edge, leaving a tiny hinge at the armhole. Cut line 3 to the bust point, leaving a hinge there too.
Spread the side section outward at bust level by the amount needed for half the extra bust room. If the total extra needed is 4 cm, spread 2 cm on each half pattern.
The side dart opens wider and the front becomes longer at the side. Cut horizontally across the centre front section at waist level and drop it to match the new length.
Redraw the darts to the bust point (shortened slightly so they end before it), true the side seam and waist, and check the armhole has kept its shape.

blocks.name: pushpin
blocks.caption: Each alteration pivots on a fixed point, such as the bust point, so the rest of the pattern stays balanced.

blocks.title: Choosing an alteration
items: Add width: full bust, broad back
Add length: rounded back, full tummy
Remove width: narrow shoulders
Remove length: sway back
blocks.caption: Name whether the body needs more or less width or length, then choose the matching alteration.

blocks.text: FBA on a princess pattern

On a princess pattern, the bust shaping lives in the side front panel. Add width to the side front panel at bust level, spreading the curve outward over the bust and blending back to the original line at the armhole and waist. Add a matching amount of length over the bust curve so it does not pull up, then add the same length to the centre front panel between the bust notches, or ease it in. Re-true the seam and move the bust notches.
Sway back

On the back bodice, draw a horizontal line a few centimetres above the waist, from centre back to the side seam. Fold out a wedge that is widest at centre back (the amount you pinched at the fitting, for example 1.5 cm) and tapers to nothing at the side seam. Redraw the centre back as a straight line; if the centre back is on a fold, the grain line may need to shift so the fold edge stays straight. For a gown, make the same change on the back skirt at the waist.
Sloping and square shoulders

For **sloping shoulders**, lower the shoulder point by the amount found at the fitting and redraw the shoulder line from the neck point. Then lower the underarm point on the side seam by the same amount, so the armhole keeps its size and the sleeve still fits. For **square shoulders**, raise both by the same amount. If only one shoulder slopes, make the change on that side only and cut the front and back as full, unfolded pieces, or use a slightly thicker shoulder pad on the low side.
Fuller upper arm

On the sleeve, draw a line down the centre from the crown to the hem, and a line across at the bicep. Cut the centre line from hem to just below the crown, then cut along the bicep line from the centre almost to each underarm point. Spread the centre line by the extra width needed; the cap drops slightly as it opens. Redraw the cap, check the new cap length against the armhole and adjust the cap ease. If the sleeve cap becomes too long, you may need to lower the underarm on the bodice slightly.

blocks.title: Worked example: altering a client's pattern after fitting
blocks.context: For example, Grace from the previous lesson has three recorded changes for her client's lace sheath gown: lower the shoulder 1 cm, FBA 2 cm each side, sway back 1.5 cm. The client also has a bicep of 36 cm and the sleeve measures 34 cm at the bicep.
steps: Shoulder: she lowers the front and back shoulder points by 1 cm and lowers the underarm by 1 cm, keeping the armhole length unchanged.
FBA: she spreads the side front panel 2 cm at bust level, blending to the armhole and waist, adds matching length over the bust and re-trues with the centre front panel.
Sway back: she folds out a 1.5 cm wedge on the back bodice and back skirt at centre back, tapering to the side.
Sleeve: she wants 3 cm of ease over the 36 cm bicep, so the sleeve needs 39 cm, which is 5 cm more than the current 34 cm. She spreads the sleeve centre by 5 cm and redraws the cap.
She measures the armhole and new sleeve cap and finds 5 cm of cap ease, more than she wants. She flattens the cap until the ease is 3 cm.
She sews a second, quick toile of the bodice and sleeve to confirm.
blocks.result: The second toile fits with no drag lines, and the client can lift her arms freely. Grace saves the altered pattern under the client's name with all amounts recorded for future orders.

blocks.title: Do not skip the second toile
blocks.text: When you make three or more changes, a second quick toile is cheaper than recutting lace. Changes interact: a lower shoulder and a wider sleeve both affect the armhole.

takeaways: Alter a copy of the pattern, pivoting on fixed points
An FBA adds width and length over the bust only
When lowering shoulders, lower the underarm to keep the armhole size
Widen sleeves by spreading, then recheck cap ease against the armhole

activity.title: Practise four alterations
steps: Make four half-scale copies of your bodice and sleeve blocks.
Perform a 2 cm FBA, a 1.5 cm sway back, a 1 cm sloping shoulder and a 4 cm upper arm alteration, one on each copy.
True all seams and recheck the armhole and cap measurements.
Label each copy with the alteration and the amount.
Write which fitting symptoms would lead you to each alteration.
activity.evidence: Photo of the four altered half-scale patterns with labels and measurements

lessons.title: Quality control for bespoke garments and production orders
objectives: Set measurement tolerances for finished garments
Build in-process checks into the sewing sequence
Run a final inspection on single garments and on batches
Record defects and use them to improve your process

blocks.text: Quality control (QC) is not one look at the end. It is a system of checks at every stage so problems are caught when they are cheap to fix. A crooked dart found before the side seams are sewn takes two minutes to correct. The same dart found after the lining and zip are in can take an hour, or may not be fixable at all on lace.
Three layers of quality control

blocks.title: Layers of quality control
items: Final inspection
In-process checks
Correct patterns and cutting
blocks.caption: Most quality is built at the bottom; the final inspection only confirms it.

items: **Correct patterns and cutting**: tested patterns, correct grain, notches cut, pieces counted against the cutting ticket.
**In-process checks**: at set points, for example after darts and before closing seams, after attaching the bodice to the skirt, after the zip.
**Final inspection**: measurements, appearance, finishing, pressing and packing.

blocks.text: Tolerances

A **tolerance** is how far a finished measurement may differ from the specification. For example, you might allow plus or minus 0.5 cm on a collar length or a bust measurement, and plus or minus 1 cm on a gown length. Tight tolerances are needed where small errors show, such as collars, cuffs and matched seams. Choose your own numbers, write them on a specification sheet for each style and measure against them, not against "looks fine".

head: Checkpoint
What to check
Example tolerance
rows: Same length, same position left and right, pressed correctly
Bust, waist, hip measured flat against the spec
Waist seams match across the zip, zip flat, no ripples
Length, sleeve length, hem level, collar symmetry
Length within 1 cm, collar points within 0.3 cm

blocks.name: inspection
blocks.caption: Inspection against written tolerances turns "looks fine" into a measurable standard.

blocks.text: Final inspection routine

items: Inspect on a dress form or hanger in good daylight or bright white light.
Outside: seams straight, prints and stripes matched, hem level, no puckers, no shine from pressing, no chalk or marker visible.
Inside: threads trimmed, seams finished, lining sitting well, no raw edges in unlined areas.
Function: zip runs smoothly, buttons secure and aligned with buttonholes, hooks fastened.
Measurements: check key measurements against the spec sheet and tolerances.
Final press, hang, cover and attach the care card.

blocks.text: Inspecting a batch

For a production order, inspect every piece if the order is small or high value, such as twenty aso-ebi gowns for one wedding. For larger repeat orders, some businesses inspect a sample from each batch and inspect everything if the sample shows problems. Large factories use formal sampling plans, but for a small workroom the safer rule is: if in doubt, inspect all. Always inspect the first garment off the line fully before sewing the rest, because a mistake in the first piece will be repeated in every piece.

Do not forget the finishing details clients notice first. Hand-sewn beads must be secured with knots every few beads, so one broken thread does not release a whole line. Hooks and eyes on a gown should sit exactly at the waist seam. Lining hems should sit about 2 to 3 cm above the outer hem so they never peep out. Labels, if you use them, should be stitched straight and flat, not scratching the neck. These small points are what separate a premium garment from an ordinary one.

blocks.title: Worked example: a defect log for an aso-ebi order
blocks.context: For example, Ronke in Ibadan and two apprentices are sewing 24 identical aso-ebi gowns for a wedding in three weeks.
steps: She fully inspects the first finished gown and finds the waist seam does not match at the zip by 0.5 cm. She corrects the sewing method before the others are sewn.
She sets checkpoints after darts, after side seams and after the zip, and adds a tick box to each bundle ticket.
At final inspection she logs defects: 3 loose threads, 2 uneven hems, 1 crooked zip.
The crooked zip and the hems are fixed. She notes that both hems came from one apprentice and shows her how to mark the hem from the floor.
Total: 24 gowns delivered on time, all passing final inspection.
blocks.result: Catching the zip issue on the first gown saved fixing 24. The defect log shows where training is needed, which improves the next order.

blocks.title: Photograph before delivery
blocks.text: Take a front, back and inside photo of every finished garment before handover. It protects you in any dispute and builds your portfolio, with the client's permission to share.

takeaways: Quality is built through patterns, in-process checks and final inspection
Write tolerances on a spec sheet and measure against them
Inspect the first garment of any batch fully before sewing the rest
Log defects and use them to improve training and methods

activity.title: Create a spec sheet and QC checklist
steps: Choose one style you sell often.
Write a spec sheet with key finished measurements and tolerances.
Add three in-process checkpoints to your sewing sequence.
Inspect one finished garment against the spec and the final inspection routine.
Start a defect log page with any issues found.
activity.evidence: Spec sheet, QC checklist and the first entry in your defect log

lessons.title: Professional client work: consultations, contracts, time-based pricing and group orders
objectives: Run a design consultation that produces a clear written brief
Price advanced work from measured time, materials and overheads
Manage deposits, payments and deadlines safely
Organise a large aso-ebi or group order without losing control

blocks.text: At advanced level, your skills are worth more, and your clients expect more: clear communication, reliable dates and garments that match what was agreed. Professional client work protects both you and the client. It turns "I thought you said" arguments into a simple check of what was written.
The design consultation

items: **Event and date**: what the garment is for, and the date it must be ready. Agree a delivery date at least a few days before the event.
**Style reference**: ask for photos and discuss what she likes in each one. Sketch the agreed design, front and back, on paper or in a phone app, and send her a photo.
**Fabric**: who supplies it, how much, whether it has been tested for shrinkage, lining choice.
**Fittings**: how many, and roughly when. Complex gowns usually need a toile fitting and at least one fitting in the real fabric.
**Price, deposit and balance**: written down, with what happens if dates or design change.

blocks.name: contract
blocks.alt: A person reviewing a contract document
blocks.caption: A short written order form protects both tailor and client.

blocks.text: The written order form

One page is enough: client name and phone, order number, design sketch or photo, fabric details, measurements reference, fitting dates, delivery date, total price, deposit paid, balance due, and your terms. Common terms include: the deposit is not refundable once fabric is cut; design changes after cutting may cost extra; late arrival for fittings may move the delivery date. Send it on WhatsApp and ask the client to reply "agreed". That message is your record.
Pricing from measured time

Advanced pieces vary too much for a fixed price list. Price from **time, materials and overheads**. Time yourself on each stage of a few garments: drafting, toile, fitting, cutting, sewing, finishing. Decide an hourly rate for your skill level. Add materials you supply (lining, interfacing, zip, thread, beads), and a share of overheads such as power, fuel, rent and machine repairs. Then add your profit margin.

blocks.title: Building a price
items: Profit
Overheads share
Materials you supply
Your time at an hourly rate
blocks.caption: Time is the foundation; materials, overheads and profit are added on top.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing a corset lace gown
blocks.context: For example, Nkechi in Lagos is pricing a corset lace gown with a full toile fitting. All naira amounts are approximate examples only, not market prices.
steps: From her time records: consultation and drafting 3 hours, toile and fitting 4 hours, cutting lace 3 hours, sewing and boning 12 hours, beading and finishing 6 hours. Total 28 hours.
She sets her hourly rate at 2,500 naira for this level of work: 28 times 2,500 = 70,000 naira.
Materials she supplies: lining, boning, zip, interfacing, thread, extra beads, about 25,000 naira.
Overheads share for 28 hours, including generator fuel: about 8,000 naira.
Subtotal 103,000 naira. She adds 20 percent profit: 103,000 times 1.2 = 123,600 naira, and quotes 125,000 naira.
She asks for a 60 percent deposit (75,000 naira) before cutting, with the balance at final fitting.
blocks.result: Nkechi can explain her price line by line. If a client pushes back, she can offer a simpler design with fewer hours instead of cutting her rate.

blocks.text: Track your real hourly earnings over time. If many quotes are refused, look at where your hours go before lowering your rate: a faster drafting method, a production pattern for a style you sell often, or batching similar tasks may cut hours without cutting quality. If almost every quote is accepted at once, your rate may be lower than your market will pay, so raise it gradually and watch the response.
Safe payments

blocks.title: Payment scams
blocks.text: Confirm every transfer in your own bank or wallet app (for example Moniepoint, Opay or your bank app) before releasing a garment. Never rely on a screenshot or an SMS alert alone, as both can be faked. Do not share OTPs or PINs with anyone claiming to be from your bank.
Group and aso-ebi orders

Group orders bring volume but can become chaotic. Appoint one coordinator on the client side. Set a firm last date for measurements and fabric collection, a few weeks before the event. Keep a spreadsheet with each person's name, phone, measurements date, fabric received, deposit, fitting date, balance and collection. Use your production patterns and graded sizes where styles are identical, and the QC checklist from the previous lesson for every piece. Say no politely to late additions you cannot finish well: one rushed garment can damage the reputation you have built on the rest.

takeaways: Run every consultation into a written, agreed order form
Price advanced work from measured time, materials, overheads and profit
Confirm payments in your own app, never by screenshot
Control group orders with a coordinator, deadlines and a tracking sheet

activity.title: Professional order pack
steps: Design a one-page order form with your terms.
Time yourself on each stage of one complex garment.
Price it using your hourly rate, materials, overheads and profit.
Create a group order tracking sheet with the columns from this lesson.
Write the WhatsApp message you would send a client with the order form.

quiz.q: During a toile fitting, Bimpe sees diagonal folds from the neck to the armhole and pulls across the bust. What should she fix first?
options: The shoulders, because fitting goes from the top down
The bust, because it is the biggest area
quiz.explain: Fit from the top down. Correcting the shoulder may remove some folds lower down before you decide on bust changes.

quiz.q: Diagonal pull lines radiate from the bust towards the armhole and side seam. What do they usually mean?
options: Too much room over the bust
Not enough room over the bust
quiz.explain: Drag lines point towards the problem. Pulls radiating from the bust show it needs more room, usually solved by a full bust adjustment.

quiz.q: You lower a client's shoulder point by 1 cm for sloping shoulders. What else must change to keep the sleeve fitting?
options: Lower the underarm point by 1 cm
quiz.explain: Lowering both shoulder and underarm keeps the armhole the same size, so the sleeve still fits.

quiz.q: A client's bicep is 34 cm and you want 3 cm ease. The sleeve currently measures 33 cm at the bicep. How much must you spread it?
quiz.explain: 34 + 3 = 37 cm needed. 37 minus 33 = 4 cm to spread.

quiz.q: In a batch of 20 identical gowns, when is the most important time to inspect fully?
options: After the first gown is finished, before sewing the rest
quiz.explain: A mistake in the first gown repeats in every gown. Full inspection of the first piece prevents batch-wide errors.

quiz.q: A gown takes 20 hours at 3,000 naira per hour, with 15,000 naira materials and 5,000 naira overheads (example figures). With 20 percent profit, what is the price before rounding?
A client sends a screenshot showing she has paid the balance. What should the tailor do before releasing the gown?
options: Confirm the money has arrived in her own bank or wallet app
Accept a promise to pay later
quiz.explain: Screenshots and SMS alerts can be faked. Always confirm in your own app before releasing goods.

finalQuiz.q: Which label must every finished production pattern piece carry so a cutter can place it correctly on the fabric?
finalQuiz.explain: The grain line arrow, running the full length of the piece, lets the cutter measure to the selvedge at two points and place the piece on grain.

finalQuiz.q: A cotton print shrinks 4 percent in length when washed. A gown is cut at 125 cm long from unwashed fabric. About how long might it be after the client's first wash?
finalQuiz.explain: 4 percent of 125 cm is 5 cm, so about 120 cm. Pre-wash or test before cutting.

finalQuiz.q: A client's high bust is 90 cm and full bust 102 cm. What is the best drafting approach for a fitted bodice?
options: Draft the frame from the smaller measurement and add bust room with a full bust adjustment
Draft from 102 cm with no changes
finalQuiz.explain: A large difference shows a full bust on a smaller frame. Drafting from the frame and adding bust room keeps shoulders and neckline fitting.

finalQuiz.q: Why should a seller of ready-made bubas publish a finished garment chart as well as a body chart?
options: Buyers can compare with a garment they own and see the ease
It removes the need for any body measurements
finalQuiz.explain: The garment chart shows actual item size; the difference from body size is the ease.

finalQuiz.q: On a flared skirt made from a straight block, where does the extra hem width come from?
options: From closing the waist dart so the slash opens at the hem
From cutting on the crosswise grain
finalQuiz.explain: Closing the dart opens the slash below it, turning dart volume into hem flare while the waist still fits.

finalQuiz.q: Armholes measure 22 cm front and 23 cm back. With 2.5 cm cap ease, what should the sleeve cap curve measure?
A shirt collar stand curves upward at the front. How does the collar that sits on top of the stand usually curve at the front?
options: It is always a straight rectangle
finalQuiz.explain: The stand curves up to hug the neck, while the collar curves down at the front so it folds and lies over the stand.

finalQuiz.q: A boubou must be 156 cm wide but the fabric is 116 cm wide. What is the professional solution?
options: Make the boubou narrower without telling the client
Add two symmetrical side panels totalling 40 cm plus seam allowances
Use one panel on the left only
finalQuiz.explain: 156 minus 116 = 40 cm, shared between two symmetrical side panels with seam allowances added.

finalQuiz.q: Pattern pieces total 2.7 square metres and the marker is 2 m long on 1.5 m fabric. What is the efficiency?
finalQuiz.explain: Marker area = 3 square metres. 2.7 divided by 3 times 100 = 90 percent.

finalQuiz.q: Your size chart has a 4 cm bust interval. How much does each quarter bodice pattern grow at bust level per size?
finalQuiz.explain: 4 cm divided by 4 quarters = 1 cm per quarter pattern.

finalQuiz.q: A toile shows horizontal folds just above the back waist on a client with a deep lower back curve. What alteration fits?
options: Sway back: fold out a wedge at centre back waist tapering to the side
finalQuiz.explain: This is a sway back. Folding out a wedge at centre back removes the excess length that causes the folds.

finalQuiz.q: Ronke inspects the first gown of a 24-piece aso-ebi order and finds the waist seam mismatched at the zip. Why was this check so valuable?
options: It only matters for that one gown
Fixing the method now prevents the same fault in all 24 gowns
It delays the order for no reason
Inspection is only needed at delivery
finalQuiz.explain: A fault in the first piece repeats across the batch. Catching it early saves fixing every gown later.

capstone.title: Professional pattern and fitting portfolio
capstone.brief: Design, draft, fit, grade and finish one advanced garment for a real client or model, such as a princess-line gown with set-in sleeves or a buba and tailored iro set, and present a complete portfolio: measurements and observations, patterns, toile fitting record, alterations, graded sizes, production pattern set, QC record and a priced order form.
steps: Hold a consultation and complete a written order form with sketch, fabric, dates, price and terms.
Take a full shape measurement set, figure observations and a garment check; record tolerances and cross-checks.
Draft the garment from your block using flat-pattern manipulation, including at least one drafted sleeve or collar.
Sew a toile, run a fitting in order, read drag lines and record every change with its amount.
Alter the pattern, sew a second quick toile if needed, then cut and sew the final garment.
Turn the final pattern into a labelled production pattern set and grade it one size up and one size down.
Inspect the finished garment against a spec sheet, photograph it and write a short reflection on what you would improve.
evidence: Signed or WhatsApp-agreed order form with sketch
Measurement card with shape measurements, observations and garment check
Photos of drafted pattern pieces with labels, notches and grain lines
Toile fitting photos with marked changes and a fitting record
Altered pattern and nested graded sizes with grade rule table
Spec sheet with tolerances and completed QC checklist
Front, back and inside photos of the finished garment
Pricing calculation from measured time, materials, overheads and profit
